topic:severe_malaria.name: Severe Malaria (P. falciparum)
topic:severe_malaria.overview: Life-threatening manifestation of Plasmodium falciparum infection. Nigeria bears the world's highest malaria burden. Progression from uncomplicated to severe malaria can occur within 24–48 hours in children under 5. Defined by WHO criteria: any child with P. falciparum parasitaemia + one or more severity features.

pearls.hpc_onset: Ask exactly when fever began and how quickly the child deteriorated — rapid decline over 24–48h distinguishes severe from uncomplicated malaria. The classic periodicity (tertian/quartan fever) is often absent in children.
pearls.hpc_character: Children with cerebral malaria may present with sudden-onset coma or seizures rather than the classic fever-rigor-sweat cycle seen in adults. Always ask caregivers about behaviour change, refusal to feed, and abnormal posturing.
pearls.sr_fever: Hyperparasitaemia (>2% parasitised RBCs) defines severity. Fever with ANY of: altered consciousness, respiratory distress, severe anaemia, prostration, repeated convulsions, hypoglycaemia = severe malaria until proven otherwise.
pearls.sr_seizures: Seizures in severe malaria = cerebral malaria (WHO criterion). >2 seizures in 24h despite antipyretics = cerebral malaria. Must distinguish from febrile seizures. Post-ictal period >30 mins suggests cerebral involvement.
pearls.sr_consciousness: Use Blantyre Coma Scale (BCS) in children <5: Eye (0–2) + Verbal (0–2) + Motor (0–2). BCS ≤2 = cerebral malaria. BCS correlates with mortality — document serially.
pearls.sr_jaundice: Jaundice = haemolysis of parasitised RBCs. Bilirubin >50 μmol/L (3 mg/dL) = WHO severity criterion. Associated with blackwater fever (massive haemolysis + haemoglobinuria).
pearls.exam_general: WHO severe malaria signs: prostration (unable to sit/stand unsupported), respiratory distress (deep acidotic breathing — Kussmaul pattern), severe pallor (Hb <5 g/dL), jaundice, haemoglobinuria (cola/dark urine).
pearls.exam_neuro: Cerebral malaria signs: coma (BCS ≤2), abnormal posturing (decorticate/decerebrate), absent corneal reflexes, papilloedema, retinal haemorrhages (pathognomonic on fundoscopy). Neck stiffness may occur — do LP only after excluding raised ICP.
pearls.exam_abdomen: Hepatosplenomegaly: spleen graded Hackett 0–5. Massively enlarged spleen (Hackett 4–5) = hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly (HMS). Spleen is soft and tender in acute malaria — handle gently (rupture risk).
pearls.ix_fbc: Hallmark findings: anaemia (Hb <5 g/dL = severe), thrombocytopaenia (platelets <150 × 10⁹/L — almost universal), normal/raised WBC. Severe anaemia + respiratory distress = transfusion threshold. MCV usually normal.
pearls.ix_rdt: HRP-2-based RDT: sensitivity ~95% for P. falciparum. Can remain positive 2 weeks post-treatment. A positive RDT + altered consciousness = start IV artesunate immediately — do NOT wait for blood film.
pearls.ix_thickfilm: Gold standard: thick film (species ID + parasitaemia quantification). Giemsa stain. >2% parasitaemia = hyperparasitaemia = WHO severity criterion. Multiple ring forms + banana-shaped gametocytes = P. falciparum.
pearls.ix_lft: Raised bilirubin (unconjugated — haemolytic). AST/ALT mildly elevated. LDH markedly elevated (haemolysis marker). Hypoglycaemia: glucose <2.2 mmol/L = WHO criterion — check BGL every 4h.
pearls.pmh_general: Ask about: prior malaria episodes, previous severe malaria/cerebral malaria (↑ risk of neurological sequelae), sickle cell disease (↑ severity), G6PD deficiency (haemolysis risk with primaquine), HIV (↑ severity and complications).
pearls.meds_general: First-line: IV artesunate (2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24h then daily). NOT IV quinine (inferior, more toxic). Step-down to oral ACT (artemether-lumefantrine) when able to tolerate oral medication. Add rectal artesunate pre-referral if IV not immediately available.
pearls.shx_travel: Exposure history: rural/peri-urban Nigeria (all high-risk), sleeping without treated net, outdoor activities at dusk/dawn. Incubation P. falciparum: 7–14 days. Ask about malaria prophylaxis compliance.
pearls.immunisation: RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix) and R21/Matrix-M vaccines: WHO-recommended for children in high-transmission areas. Nigeria rolling out R21. Vaccine reduces severe malaria by ~75% but is not a replacement for other prevention measures.

laboratory: Thick and thin blood film (Giemsa stain) — parasitaemia quantification
Renal profile — AKI in severe malaria
imaging: CT head — only if LP being considered with focal neurology
investigations.key_findings: Hb <5 g/dL = severe anaemia (transfuse if RD present). Glucose <2.2 mmol/L = hypoglycaemia (IV dextrose immediately). Parasitaemia >2% = hyperparasitaemia. Metabolic acidosis (base deficit >8) = poor prognosis marker.

differentials.distinguishing: CSF pleocytosis, elevated protein; purpuric rash; blood film negative for malaria

differentials.name: Viral Encephalitis
differentials.distinguishing: CSF lymphocytosis; malaria film/RDT negative; slower onset

differentials.name: Febrile Seizure
differentials.distinguishing: Age 6mo–5yr; brief (<15 min); no post-ictal coma; BCS normal after seizure

differentials.name: Typhoid Fever

differentials.name: Septicaemia

topic:severe_malaria.management_pearls: IV artesunate is first-line (superior to quinine in all trials). Start oxygen. IV 10% dextrose for hypoglycaemia. Blood transfusion: Hb <5 g/dL with RD, or Hb <4 g/dL regardless. Phenobarbitone 15–20 mg/kg IV for seizure prophylaxis in cerebral malaria (controversial — discuss with senior). Nurse semi-prone. Monitor BCS, BGL, and urine output hourly.
topic:severe_malaria.nigerian_context: FMOH first-line: IV artesunate for severe malaria. Rectal artesunate (10 mg/kg) for pre-referral treatment when IV not available. Avoid quinine (QTc prolongation, hypoglycaemia). Chloroquine resistance is near-universal in Nigeria.

topic:bacterial_meningitis.name: Bacterial Meningitis
topic:bacterial_meningitis.overview: Bacterial infection of the meninges — a paediatric emergency with significant mortality (10–20%) and neurological sequelae in survivors (deafness, cerebral palsy, cognitive impairment). Most common organisms by age: neonates (<1mo) — GBS, E. coli, Listeria; infants/children — S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae.

pearls.hpc_onset: Classical triad (fever + headache + neck stiffness) present in only 44% of children. In infants: bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry, and poor feeding may be the only signs. Rapid progression (hours) favours meningococcal disease.
pearls.hpc_character: Headache in older children is severe and 'worst of life'. Photophobia and phonophobia are common. Progressive drowsiness is an ominous sign — document GCS/AVPU serially.
pearls.sr_fever: Fever + petechial/purpuric rash = meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise — give IV ceftriaxone IMMEDIATELY (before LP, before imaging). Do not delay for investigations.
pearls.sr_seizures: Seizures in meningitis: focal seizure = cortical involvement/venous thrombosis. Prolonged post-ictal state = raised ICP. Treat with IV diazepam; avoid repeated benzodiazepines (respiratory depression).
pearls.exam_neuro: Meningeal signs: Kernig's (pain on knee extension with hip flexed 90°), Brudzinski's (passive neck flexion → involuntary hip flexion). Sensitivity low in infants — bulging fontanelle is more reliable under 18 months. Papilloedema = raised ICP — do NOT do LP.
pearls.exam_general: Rash: petechiae (non-blanching) = meningococcal until proven otherwise — do NOT wait for CSF. Mottled skin, capillary refill >2s, cold peripheries = septic shock — resuscitate first.
pearls.ix_fbc: WBC usually elevated (>15 × 10⁹/L, neutrophil predominance). Thrombocytopaenia in meningococcal septicaemia (DIC). Blood culture: positive in 50–80% — take BEFORE antibiotics if possible (but do NOT delay antibiotics).
pearls.ix_lft: CRP >100 mg/L strongly suggests bacterial aetiology. Procalcitonin >2 ng/mL also favours bacterial meningitis. Electrolytes: hyponatraemia (SIADH — common complication, restrict fluids).
pearls.pmh_general: Risk factors: sickle cell disease (functional asplenia → pneumococcal risk), HIV, immunodeficiency, cochlear implants, CSF leak, previous meningitis. Vaccination history is critical — Hib, PCV, MenC vaccines reduce risk significantly.
pearls.immunisation: Nigerian EPI: PCV13 at 6/10/14 weeks reduces pneumococcal meningitis. Hib vaccine reduces H. influenzae meningitis. MenACWY not yet in routine EPI — high-risk groups only. Meningococcal belt: Nigeria high risk for MenA (epidemic season Dec–June).

signs: Papilloedema (raised ICP — contraindication to immediate LP)

bedside: Blood culture (take before antibiotics if possible)
laboratory: Lumbar puncture (CSF) — ONLY after excluding raised ICP

csf_findings.bacterial: Turbid/purulent CSF. WBC >1000 (neutrophil predominance). Protein >1.5 g/L. Glucose <2.2 mmol/L (or CSF:blood glucose ratio <0.6). Gram stain positive in 60–80%. Culture positive in 70–85%.
csf_findings.viral: Clear CSF. WBC 10–1000 (lymphocyte predominance). Protein mildly elevated. Glucose normal.
csf_findings.contraindications_to_lp: Papilloedema, focal neurology, GCS <13, coagulopathy, skin infection at LP site, cardiovascular instability. Give antibiotics first, do CT, then LP.

imaging: CT head (before LP if raised ICP suspected)
MRI brain (complications: abscess, subdural empyema, venous thrombosis)
investigations.key_findings: CSF turbid + neutrophilia + low glucose + high protein = bacterial meningitis. Latex agglutination (CSF) for rapid antigen detection. PCR for N. meningitidis / S. pneumoniae in CSF.

differentials.name: Viral Meningitis / Encephalitis
differentials.distinguishing: Clear CSF; lymphocytes; normal glucose; less toxic-looking child

differentials.name: Cerebral Malaria
differentials.distinguishing: Malaria parasites on blood film; RDT positive; no CSF pleocytosis

differentials.name: Tuberculous Meningitis
differentials.distinguishing: Subacute onset; CSF lymphocytosis + very low glucose + fibrin web; AFB on CSF; chest X-ray changes

differentials.name: Brain Abscess
differentials.distinguishing: Focal signs; fever; CT shows ring-enhancing lesion; no CSF pleocytosis (LP often contraindicated)

differentials.name: Febrile Seizure
differentials.distinguishing: Age 6mo–5yr; brief; no meningism; normal after seizure

topic:bacterial_meningitis.management_pearls: Give IV ceftriaxone (100 mg/kg/day) immediately — before LP if petechial rash present or child is deteriorating. Add ampicillin if <3 months (Listeria cover). Dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg 6-hourly × 4 days) — reduces deafness in Hib and pneumococcal meningitis; give with or before first antibiotic dose. Monitor for complications: SIADH (restrict fluids), DIC, subdural empyema, hearing loss. Audiology review before discharge.

topic:typhoid_fever.name: Typhoid Fever (Enteric Fever)
topic:typhoid_fever.overview: Systemic infection caused by Salmonella enterica typhi (typhoid) or S. paratyphi (paratyphoid). Common in Nigeria due to poor sanitation and contaminated water. Incubation: 7–21 days. Older children present more classically; infants may have nonspecific illness.

pearls.hpc_onset: Stepwise rising fever over 1 week is the classic pattern — but often not seen in practice. Ask about: contaminated water/food exposure, swimming in rivers, travel to endemic areas, other family members affected.
pearls.sr_fever: Relative bradycardia (pulse-temperature dissociation): fever >39°C but HR lower than expected. Highly specific but present in only 30% of cases. Continuous fever (remittent, not intermittent) distinguishes from malaria.
pearls.exam_abdomen: Rose spots (2–3mm blanching salmon-pink macules on trunk): pathognomonic, but seen in only 20–30% and difficult to see on dark skin. Soft splenomegaly (in 50%). Hepatomegaly. Abdominal distension — intestinal ileus.
pearls.ix_fbc: Leucopaenia (WBC <4 × 10⁹/L) with relative lymphocytosis — characteristic finding that helps distinguish from bacterial infections. Thrombocytopaenia in severe cases. CRP elevated.
pearls.ix_lft: Blood culture (gold standard): positive in 60–80% in first week. Widal test: limitations — cross-reactions, previous vaccination, endemic area baseline titres. O antigen >1:160 and H antigen >1:160 are suggestive but not diagnostic. Typhidot IgM more sensitive.
pearls.pmh_general: Complications: intestinal perforation (RIF pain → peritonitis — surgical emergency), intestinal haemorrhage, toxic encephalopathy ('typhoid state'), myocarditis, hepatitis, relapse (10%).

symptoms: Stepwise rising fever (1st week: low-grade; 2nd week: high plateau)
Altered consciousness / delirium in severe cases
signs: Rose spots (trunk — 20–30%, difficult on dark skin)

laboratory: Blood culture (gold standard — 60–80% positive in week 1)
Widal test (limitations noted — use with clinical context)
Bone marrow culture (most sensitive — 90%, used when blood culture negative)
imaging: Abdominal X-ray — perforation: air under diaphragm (erect CXR/AXR)
investigations.key_findings: Blood culture positive = definitive diagnosis. Leucopaenia + fever + relative bradycardia + endemic area = treat empirically while awaiting culture.

differentials.name: Malaria
differentials.distinguishing: Positive blood film/RDT; intermittent fever pattern; no relative bradycardia

differentials.name: Bacterial Meningitis
differentials.distinguishing: Meningism; CSF findings; leucocytosis

differentials.name: Viral Hepatitis
differentials.distinguishing: Marked jaundice; very high transaminases; LFT pattern

differentials.name: Brucellosis
differentials.distinguishing: Animal contact; undulant fever; positive serology/culture

differentials.name: Leptospirosis
differentials.distinguishing: Water/animal exposure; conjunctival suffusion; elevated creatinine

topic:typhoid_fever.management_pearls: First-line: azithromycin (20 mg/kg/day × 7 days) — excellent oral bioavailability, fewer resistance concerns. Fluoroquinolone resistance common in Nigeria. Ceftriaxone (60 mg/kg/day IV) for severe/complicated typhoid. Perforation: emergency surgical exploration + ceftriaxone + metronidazole. Dexamethasone for toxic encephalopathy (severe cases only).

topic:measles.name: Measles
topic:measles.overview: Highly contagious paramyxovirus infection. R₀ of 12–18 (most infectious of all human pathogens). Remains a leading cause of child mortality in Nigeria due to incomplete vaccination coverage. Complications are the main cause of death — pneumonia, encephalitis, severe malnutrition.

pearls.hpc_onset: 3 Cs + fever for 2–4 days BEFORE rash: Cough, Coryza (runny nose), Conjunctivitis. Koplik's spots (pathognomonic) appear 1–2 days before rash — small white spots on bright red buccal mucosa opposite lower molars.
pearls.sr_fever: High fever (>40°C) throughout prodrome and during rash. Fever that falls then rises again = secondary bacterial infection (pneumonia). Persistent fever >5 days after rash onset = complication.
pearls.exam_skin: Maculopapular rash: begins behind ears → face → trunk → limbs. Coalesces centrally. Brick-red/brownish. Blanches on pressure (early) — may become haemorrhagic in severe disease. Rash lasts 5–7 days, then desquamates.
pearls.exam_general: Check for complications: tachypnoea/chest recession (pneumonia), photophobia/meningism (encephalitis), severe eye discharge + corneal clouding (keratoconjunctivitis → blindness), mouth ulcers + wasting (complicated malnutrition).
pearls.ix_fbc: Leucopaenia (lymphopaenia) — characteristic. Lymphocyte count often <1 × 10⁹/L. Measles causes profound immunosuppression lasting 2–3 years ('immune amnesia') — increases susceptibility to all infections.
pearls.immunisation: Two doses of MCV: MCV1 at 9 months, MCV2 at 12–15 months (Nigerian EPI). Outbreak dose: MCV to all children 6 months–15 years regardless of history. Vitamin A supplementation: 200,000 IU for all children >12 months with measles — reduces mortality by 50%.
pearls.meds_general: Vitamin A (reduces mortality and blindness): <6 months: 50,000 IU. 6–11 months: 100,000 IU. >12 months: 200,000 IU — give on days 1 and 2. Antibiotics only for bacterial complications. Antivirals: ribavirin in immunocompromised (specialist use).

signs: Koplik's spots (pathognomonic — buccal mucosa opposite lower molars)

complications: Pneumonia (most common cause of death — bacterial superinfection: S. pneumoniae, S. aureus)

differentials.name: Rubella
differentials.distinguishing: Milder; suboccipital lymphadenopathy; no Koplik's; rash finer; lasts only 3 days

differentials.name: Roseola Infantum (HHV-6)
differentials.distinguishing: Rash appears AS fever breaks; age <2 years; no 3 Cs

differentials.name: Dengue Fever
differentials.distinguishing: Thrombocytopaenia; haemorrhagic tendency; positive NS1 antigen; no Koplik's

differentials.name: Drug Reaction (Steven-Johnson)
differentials.distinguishing: Drug exposure; mucous membrane involvement; no Koplik's; acral blistering

differentials.name: Scarlet Fever
differentials.distinguishing: Sandpaper rash; strawberry tongue; throat culture positive; no Koplik's

topic:tuberculosis_child.name: Childhood Tuberculosis
topic:tuberculosis_child.overview: Nigeria is a TB high-burden country (top 8 globally). Primary TB in children usually results from household contact with an infectious adult. Pulmonary TB most common; extra-pulmonary (TB meningitis, miliary, abdominal, lymphadenopathy) more common in children <5 and immunocompromised.

pearls.hpc_onset: Subacute or chronic onset (>2 weeks). The key questions: (1) household contact with TB case or chronic cougher, (2) duration of symptoms, (3) weight loss trajectory. TB should be suspected in any child with symptoms >2 weeks despite antibiotics.
pearls.sr_fever: Low-grade fever, often worse in the evening ('evening rise of temperature'). Night sweats. Weight loss. The triad of chronic cough + fever + weight loss in a child = TB until proven otherwise in Nigeria.
pearls.exam_general: Wasting and failure to thrive. Cervical lymphadenopathy (matted, non-tender nodes — 'collar-stud abscess' if fluctuant). BCG scar — its presence does not exclude TB. MUAC and weight for age.
pearls.exam_chest: Pulmonary TB in children: often few chest signs. May have reduced air entry, dullness to percussion over consolidation. Wheeze if endobronchial TB compressing bronchus (especially hilar lymph nodes).
pearls.ix_fbc: Non-specific: normocytic anaemia, elevated ESR and CRP. Tuberculin skin test (TST/Mantoux): ≥10mm induration in non-immunocompromised = significant. ≥5mm in HIV-positive child. May be negative in severe malnutrition, miliary TB, or immunosuppression (anergy).
pearls.ix_cxr: Chest X-ray: hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy (most common finding in primary TB), consolidation, cavitation (post-primary), miliary pattern (1–2mm nodules throughout both lungs = disseminated TB), pleural effusion.
pearls.pmh_general: HIV co-infection dramatically increases TB risk and worsens outcomes. All children with TB should be tested for HIV. BCG vaccination protects against miliary TB and TB meningitis (not pulmonary TB).
pearls.shx_travel: Close contact with smear-positive adult = main transmission route. Overcrowded housing, poor ventilation. Household contact investigation (index case) is essential.
pearls.ix_lft: Sputum/gastric lavage AFB smear (children often cannot expectorate — early morning gastric aspirate × 3 consecutive days). GeneXpert MTB/RIF (rapid diagnosis + rifampicin resistance in 2 hours) — preferred over AFB smear. Culture: gold standard but 6–8 weeks.

laboratory: Sputum or gastric aspirate: AFB smear, GeneXpert MTB/RIF, culture
Liver function tests (baseline before starting ATT)
imaging: CXR — hilar lymphadenopathy, consolidation, miliary pattern
investigations.key_findings: GeneXpert positive = confirmed TB. In children, clinical scoring (Keith Edwards score / Stegen-Toledo) used when bacteriological confirmation not possible. Hilar lymphadenopathy on CXR + positive Mantoux + household contact = probable TB.

differentials.name: Bacterial Pneumonia
differentials.distinguishing: Acute onset; responds to antibiotics; no household TB contact; CXR: lobar/segmental

differentials.name: Lymphoma
differentials.distinguishing: Painless mediastinal/cervical LN; night sweats; CXR: widened mediastinum; biopsy

differentials.name: HIV-related lung disease
differentials.distinguishing: HIV positive; bilateral interstitial infiltrates; PCP pneumonia; no response to ATT alone

differentials.name: Sarcoidosis
differentials.distinguishing: Rare in children; bilateral hilar LN; elevated ACE; negative Mantoux

differentials.name: Malnutrition
differentials.distinguishing: Weight loss and wasting without fever; no household contact; Mantoux negative

topic:tuberculosis_child.management_pearls: Paediatric ATT (HRZE): Isoniazid + Rifampicin + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol × 2 months, then HR × 4 months (6 months total). Weight-based dosing — adjust monthly. Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) with isoniazid in malnourished/HIV+. All children aged <5 and HIV+ close contacts of smear-positive TB: isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) 6 months. DOTS (directly observed therapy) improves adherence.

topic:severe_acute_malnutrition.name: Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM)
topic:severe_acute_malnutrition.overview: SAM is defined by WHO as MUAC <11.5cm, OR weight-for-height z-score (WHZ) <−3, OR bilateral pitting oedema (kwashiorkor). Affects children primarily 6–59 months. Nigeria has one of the highest burdens globally. Major risk: refeeding syndrome, overwhelming sepsis (hypothermia, hypoglycaemia), death.

pearls.exam_general: SAM criteria: MUAC <11.5cm OR WHZ <−3 OR bilateral pitting oedema. Always check bilateral pitting pretibial oedema — its presence = kwashiorkor regardless of weight. Kwashiorkor is caused by severe protein deficiency, not just caloric deficit.
pearls.sr_fever: Hypothermia (<35.5°C) is as dangerous as hyperthermia in SAM — impaired thermoregulation. Fever may be absent even with serious infection. Always check blood glucose: hypoglycaemia (<3 mmol/L) is a medical emergency in SAM.
pearls.ix_fbc: Anaemia is almost universal (multifactorial: iron, folate, B12 deficiency + chronic infection + malaria). Leucopaenia may occur. Infection: WBC may NOT be elevated — immunosuppression is profound. Blood culture important even without obvious infection.
pearls.exam_skin: Kwashiorkor skin changes: 'flaky paint' dermatosis (hyperpigmented plaques that peel), hypopigmented patches, skin breakdown, ulceration. Hair changes: sparse, reddish/brownish, easily plucked without pain ('flag sign'). Oedema: bilateral pitting of feet/ankles — ascends in severe cases.
pearls.hpc_character: Marasmus: severe wasting — 'skin and bones'. Muscle wasting exposes ribs, spine, and scapulae. 'Old man facies' (loss of buccal fat). Marasmic kwashiorkor: features of both. Always ask about duration of food reduction and recent illness (accelerating trigger).
pearls.meds_general: F-75 (starter formula, 75 kcal/100mL) for first 1–2 weeks: 100 kcal/kg/day. Transition to F-100 (100 kcal/100mL) cautiously (refeeding syndrome risk). RUTF (Plumpy'Nut) for uncomplicated SAM outpatient management (CMAM). Routine: antibiotics (amoxicillin), folic acid, Vitamin A, zinc.
pearls.pmh_general: Always investigate for underlying cause: HIV (CD4 count), TB (household contact, TST), persistent diarrhoea, congenital heart disease, chronic illness. SAM in an older child (>5 years) without obvious cause: strongly consider HIV or TB.

marasmus: Severe wasting — visible ribs, scapulae, vertebrae
Loss of buccal fat pad ('old man facies')
kwashiorkor: Weight may appear normal due to oedema

laboratory: Blood culture (sepsis common, fever may be absent)
imaging: CXR — TB, pneumonia, cardiomegaly (from nutritional cardiomyopathy)
investigations.key_findings: Hypoglycaemia + hypothermia + infection = the lethal triad in SAM. Refeeding syndrome: dangerous drop in phosphate/potassium/magnesium when nutrition reintroduced too rapidly — monitor electrolytes daily in refeeding phase.

differentials.name: Nephrotic Syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Oedema + massive proteinuria + hypoalbuminaemia; urine dipstick 3+ protein; no wasting

differentials.name: Congestive Heart Failure
differentials.distinguishing: Oedema + cardiac signs; hepatomegaly + raised JVP; CXR cardiomegaly

differentials.name: Kwashiorkor vs Marasmus
differentials.distinguishing: Oedema = kwashiorkor regardless of weight. Wasting without oedema = marasmus. Both = marasmic kwashiorkor

differentials.name: HIV Wasting Syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: HIV positive; chronic diarrhoea; opportunistic infections; older age group

differentials.name: Chronic Illness (TB, CHD)
differentials.distinguishing: Underlying disease features; investigate in all SAM cases not responding to treatment

topic:pneumonia_child.name: Childhood Pneumonia
topic:pneumonia_child.overview: Leading infectious cause of child mortality globally and in Nigeria. Defined as infection of the lung parenchyma. WHO classifies by severity: fast breathing (non-severe) → chest indrawing (severe) → general danger signs (very severe). Most common causative organisms: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae type b, S. aureus, viral (RSV, influenza, parainfluenza).

pearls.hpc_onset: Age-specific aetiology: neonates — GBS, gram-negatives. Infants <2 months — S. aureus, gram-negatives, Chlamydia. 2 months–5 years — S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae. >5 years — S. pneumoniae, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia pneumoniae.
pearls.sr_fever: WHO fast breathing thresholds (per minute): <2 months: ≥60. 2–11 months: ≥50. 1–5 years: ≥40. >5 years: ≥30. Count respiratory rate for ONE FULL MINUTE when child is calm — this is the most sensitive sign.
pearls.exam_chest: Danger signs (IMCI): chest indrawing (lower chest wall drawing IN on inspiration), stridor at rest, central cyanosis, grunting, severe respiratory distress. Auscultation: reduced air entry, bronchial breathing, fine inspiratory crackles. Percussion: dullness (consolidation/effusion).
pearls.exam_general: IMCI danger signs = very severe pneumonia: unable to drink/breastfeed, persistent vomiting, convulsions, lethargic/unconscious, cyanosis, severe respiratory distress, SpO₂ <90%. All require immediate hospital admission and oxygen.
pearls.ix_cxr: CXR findings: lobar/segmental consolidation (bacterial), round pneumonia (S. pneumoniae), bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates (viral/Mycoplasma/PCP), pleural effusion, pneumatocele (S. aureus), cavitation (TB, S. aureus).
pearls.ix_fbc: WBC >15 × 10⁹/L + neutrophilia = bacterial aetiology. Normal/low WBC + lymphocytosis = viral. CRP >80 mg/L favours bacterial. Blood culture: positive in only 10–15% of bacterial pneumonia — but essential in severe cases.
pearls.meds_general: Outpatient (non-severe): amoxicillin 40 mg/kg/day × 5 days. Hospital (severe): IV ampicillin + gentamicin (FMOH guideline). Suspected staphylococcal (S. aureus — pneumatocele, rapid progression): add cloxacillin/flucloxacillin. Oxygen for SpO₂ <90%.

who_classification.fast_breathing_only: Non-severe pneumonia — treat with oral amoxicillin as outpatient
who_classification.chest_indrawing: Severe pneumonia — admit + IV antibiotics + oxygen
who_classification.danger_signs: Very severe pneumonia — emergency admission + oxygen + IV antibiotics + supportive care

differentials.name: Bronchiolitis
differentials.distinguishing: Age <2 years; RSV; wheeze + hyperinflation; fine crackles; no consolidation on CXR

differentials.name: Asthma Exacerbation
differentials.distinguishing: Wheeze; response to bronchodilators; history of atopy; no fever (usually)

differentials.name: Pulmonary TB
differentials.distinguishing: Chronic cough >2 weeks; household TB contact; hilar LN on CXR; AFB/GeneXpert

differentials.name: Heart Failure
differentials.distinguishing: Cardiomegaly on CXR; gallop rhythm; JVP raised; oedema

differentials.name: Foreign Body Aspiration
differentials.distinguishing: Sudden onset; no fever; asymmetric wheeze; history of choking episode

topic:gastroenteritis_child.name: Acute Gastroenteritis & Dehydration
topic:gastroenteritis_child.overview: Diarrhoea is a leading cause of child death in Nigeria. Defined as ≥3 loose stools in 24h. Rotavirus is the most common cause of severe gastroenteritis in children under 5. Dehydration is the primary cause of death. Accurate dehydration assessment and appropriate rehydration therapy are the key clinical skills.

pearls.hpc_onset: Duration classifies: acute (<14 days), persistent (14–30 days), chronic (>30 days). Ask: blood in stool (dysentery → Shigella, EHEC, Entamoeba), vomiting pattern, urine output (quantifies dehydration), weight before illness.
pearls.hpc_character: Rice-water stools = cholera until proven otherwise (epidemic context). Bloody mucoid stools = dysentery (Shigella most common in Nigeria). Explosive watery diarrhoea in groups = Salmonella, viral. Greasy offensive stools = Giardia.
pearls.exam_general: WHO dehydration assessment: No dehydration → Some dehydration → Severe dehydration. Key signs: skin turgor (pinch abdominal skin — slow return >2s = moderate dehydration), sunken eyes, sunken fontanelle, dry mouth/tongue, lethargy, deep rapid breathing (acidosis), capillary refill >3s (severe).
pearls.sr_urinary: Urine output is the best practical guide: no wet nappy for >6–8h in infants = significant dehydration. Dark concentrated urine. Oliguria progressing to anuria in severe dehydration/HUS.
pearls.ix_fbc: Stool microscopy: RBCs + WBCs = dysentery (bacterial). Cysts = Giardia/Entamoeba. Stool culture (Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter). Electrolytes: hyper/hyponatraemia (dangerous dehydration variants). Renal profile: rising creatinine in HUS (haemolytic uraemic syndrome — E. coli O157:H7).
pearls.meds_general: ORS (low osmolality WHO-ORS): cornerstone of treatment. Zinc supplementation (10mg/day <6 months; 20mg/day >6 months × 10–14 days) reduces duration and recurrence. Antibiotics: ONLY for dysentery (ciprofloxacin/azithromycin) and cholera. NO antimotility agents in children. Continue breastfeeding throughout.

dehydration_signs.no_dehydration: Alert, normal eyes, moist mouth, normal skin turgor, normal fontanelle
dehydration_signs.some_dehydration: Restless/irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly/thirsty, dry mouth, slow skin return (<2s), sunken fontanelle
dehydration_signs.severe_dehydration: Lethargic/unconscious, very sunken eyes, unable to drink, very dry mouth, skin return >2s, deeply sunken fontanelle, capillary refill >3s

investigations.key_findings: Hyponatraemia + seizures = hyponatraemic dehydration (dangerous — correct sodium slowly). Hypernatraemia = hypernatraemic dehydration (doughy skin feel; correcting too fast causes cerebral oedema). Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopaenia + AKI = HUS.

differentials.name: Intussusception
differentials.distinguishing: Intermittent colicky pain; 'redcurrant jelly' stool; sausage-shaped mass RUQ; USS target sign

differentials.name: Appendicitis
differentials.distinguishing: RIF pain; guarding; rebound; no diarrhoea early; Alvarado score

differentials.name: Septicaemia
differentials.distinguishing: Shock disproportionate to diarrhoea; positive blood culture; fever + toxicity

differentials.name: DKA
differentials.distinguishing: Hyperglycaemia; ketones in breath/urine; Kussmaul breathing; no infectious diarrhoea

who_plan.plan_a: No dehydration: ORS at home, continue feeding, return if worse. 5–10 mL/kg after each loose stool.
who_plan.plan_b: Some dehydration: 75 mL/kg ORS over 4 hours in health facility, reassess.
who_plan.plan_c: Severe dehydration: IV Ringer's Lactate 100 mL/kg over 3h (<12mo) or 3h (>12mo). Reassess every 30 min.

topic:febrile_seizure.name: Febrile Seizure
topic:febrile_seizure.overview: Seizure associated with fever (>38°C) in a neurologically normal child aged 6 months to 5 years, without evidence of CNS infection or other cause. Most common seizure disorder in childhood — affects 2–5% of children. Benign in the vast majority. Key risk: distinguishing from meningitis/encephalitis.

pearls.hpc_onset: Simple febrile seizure: occurs in first 24h of fever, generalised tonic-clonic, lasts <15 minutes, single episode, complete recovery. Complex febrile seizure: focal, >15 minutes, occurs >1 in 24h, or post-ictal deficit — needs thorough investigation.
pearls.sr_seizures: Description of seizure is critical: Was it generalised or one-sided? How long did it last? Did the child recover fully and quickly? Focal seizure = structural cause must be excluded. Duration >15 min = status epilepticus — IV diazepam 0.3 mg/kg.
pearls.sr_fever: Cause of fever must be identified: common sources are URTI, otitis media, tonsillitis, UTI, roseola. The fever itself, not the rate of temperature rise, is the trigger.
pearls.exam_neuro: After the seizure: is the child fully alert? Focal deficit? Meningism? If post-ictal GCS <15 persisting >1 hour, or any meningism → LP mandatory. A child who recovers quickly and is alert with no meningism = simple febrile seizure.
pearls.pmh_general: Recurrence risk: 30–35% will have another febrile seizure. Risk factors for recurrence: age <18 months at first episode, family history, low-grade fever at seizure onset, short duration of fever before seizure.
pearls.meds_general: Acute: IV/rectal diazepam for seizure >5 minutes. Paracetamol for fever control (does NOT prevent recurrence). No routine prophylactic anticonvulsants. Educate parents: rectal diazepam at home for seizure >5 minutes before bringing to hospital.

differentials.name: Bacterial Meningitis
differentials.distinguishing: Meningism; purpuric rash; no post-ictal recovery; CSF findings

differentials.name: Cerebral Malaria
differentials.distinguishing: BCS ≤2; positive blood film/RDT; prolonged impaired consciousness

differentials.name: Epilepsy
differentials.distinguishing: No fever; recurrent; afebrile episodes; EEG abnormality

differentials.name: Hypoglycaemic Seizure
differentials.distinguishing: Blood glucose <2.2 mmol/L; known DM or SAM; corrects with dextrose

differentials.name: Encephalitis
differentials.distinguishing: Altered consciousness persisting; CSF pleocytosis; EEG changes

topic:neonatal_sepsis.name: Neonatal Sepsis
topic:neonatal_sepsis.overview: Bacterial infection in the first 28 days of life. Early-onset sepsis (EOS): first 72h of life — maternal organisms (GBS, E. coli, Listeria). Late-onset sepsis (LOS): day 4–28 — nosocomial organisms (Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella, E. coli, coagulase-negative Staph). Leading cause of neonatal mortality in Nigeria.

pearls.hpc_onset: EOS risk factors: prolonged rupture of membranes (PROM >18h), maternal fever in labour, Group B Strep colonisation, preterm birth, perinatal asphyxia. LOS risk factors: prematurity, invasive lines/procedures, overcrowded NICU.
pearls.hpc_character: Classic neonatal sepsis presentation: the baby 'looks sick' — lethargic, poor feeding, temperature instability (hypothermia OR hyperthermia). Non-specific signs: jitteriness, colour change, respiratory distress, apnoea, abdominal distension.
pearls.sr_fever: CRITICAL: Neonates may be HYPOTHERMIC (not febrile) with sepsis — impaired thermoregulation. Temperature instability (either direction) = treat as sepsis. A neonate with hypothermia (<36.5°C) must have blood culture and start empirical antibiotics.
pearls.exam_general: Danger signs: poor tone/floppiness, bulging fontanelle, respiratory distress, grunting, apnoea, poor perfusion (pallor, mottling, CRT >3s), jaundice in first 24h, purpuric skin lesions.
pearls.ix_fbc: FBC: leucocytosis (>25 × 10⁹/L) OR leucopaenia (<5 × 10⁹/L). I:T ratio (immature:total neutrophils) >0.2 = significant. Thrombocytopaenia <100 = DIC risk. CRP >10 mg/L at 24h of age.
pearls.ix_lft: Blood culture (gold standard — take before antibiotics). Lumbar puncture: mandatory if meningitis suspected (bulging fontanelle, focal neurology, positive blood culture). CSF: neonatal normals different — protein up to 1.5 g/L, WBC up to 30 cells. Sepsis screen: FBC + CRP + blood culture ± CSF.
pearls.meds_general: Empirical: IV ampicillin + gentamicin (EOS). Adjust based on culture sensitivity. LOS/nosocomial: consider adding gram-positive cover (flucloxacillin, vancomycin in MRSA-endemic units). Duration: bacteraemia 7–10 days; meningitis 14–21 days.

differentials.name: Neonatal Meningitis
differentials.distinguishing: Often concurrent with sepsis; bulging fontanelle; seizures; CSF abnormal

differentials.name: Perinatal Asphyxia (HIE)
differentials.distinguishing: Depressed Apgar scores; encephalopathy; no fever/temperature instability; normal blood culture

differentials.name: Metabolic Disease (IEM)
differentials.distinguishing: Encephalopathy; abnormal metabolic screen; family history; specific metabolite testing

differentials.name: Congenital Heart Disease
differentials.distinguishing: Murmur; cyanosis not improving with O₂; CXR cardiomegaly; ECHO

differentials.name: Neonatal Jaundice
differentials.distinguishing: Jaundice alone (Coombs test, G6PD deficiency) vs sepsis with jaundice

topic:sickle_cell_disease_child.name: Sickle Cell Disease — Paediatric Complications
topic:sickle_cell_disease_child.overview: HbSS is the most common severe monogenic disorder in Nigeria — approximately 150,000 affected children born annually. Sickle cell disease causes multi-system complications from red cell sickling and vaso-occlusion. Key paediatric emergencies: vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC), acute chest syndrome (ACS), splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis, stroke.

pearls.hpc_onset: Vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC): symmetrical dactylitis ('hand-foot syndrome') in first presentation aged 6–24 months. Bone pain crises begin after physiological HbF decline at 6 months. Ask about precipitants: cold, dehydration, infection, hypoxia, stress.
pearls.hpc_character: Pain crisis: severe, constant, bone pain — most commonly back, chest, limbs. Acute chest syndrome: new pulmonary infiltrate + chest pain + fever + respiratory distress — can rapidly progress to respiratory failure. Splenic sequestration: sudden massive splenomegaly + haemodynamic compromise in child <5 years.
pearls.sr_fever: Any fever in SCD = bacteraemia risk (functional asplenia by age 3 years). Treat as emergency — blood culture + empirical ceftriaxone IV. Common organisms: S. pneumoniae (most feared), H. influenzae, Salmonella (osteomyelitis).
pearls.exam_general: Chronic: pallor, scleral icterus (haemolytic jaundice), frontal bossing, tower skull, delayed growth/puberty. Acute: look for spleen size (measure carefully — rapid enlargement = sequestration). Assess hydration.
pearls.exam_abdomen: Splenomegaly: in young children before autosplenectomy. Rapid enlargement = sequestration crisis (shock if large volume trapped). Autosplenectomy: by age 5–6 years the spleen is non-functional — Howell-Jolly bodies on blood film, absent spleen on USS.
pearls.exam_neuro: Stroke: occurs in 10% of HbSS patients by age 20. Any focal neurology (hemiplegia, facial droop, speech difficulty, visual loss) in SCD = EMERGENCY — exchange transfusion URGENTLY. TIA is also an indication.
pearls.ix_fbc: Baseline Hb in HbSS: 60–90 g/L (compensated chronic haemolytic anaemia). Drop of ≥20 g/L below baseline = acute anaemia. Aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19): reticulocyte count falls to <1% — severe anaemia without compensation. MCV elevated (reticulocytosis). Howell-Jolly bodies = functional asplenia.
pearls.ix_lft: Haemoglobin electrophoresis (gold standard for diagnosis): HbSS, HbSC, HbS-thal etc. Bilirubin: elevated (indirect — haemolysis). Cholelithiasis (pigment stones) common from adolescence. Ferritin elevated (transfusion iron overload).
pearls.pmh_general: Vaccinations critical (functional asplenia): PCV13, MenACWY, Hib, annual influenza. Penicillin V prophylaxis from 3 months until at least age 5 years (or lifelong). Folic acid supplementation daily. Hydroxyurea: increases HbF, reduces crisis frequency — consider in recurrent crises.
pearls.meds_general: VOC: IV morphine (titrate to pain), IV fluids (1.5× maintenance), oxygen (if SpO₂ <95%), NSAID (adjunct for bone pain in older children without renal impairment). ACS: empirical antibiotics + bronchodilators + transfusion/exchange if severe. Aplastic crisis: blood transfusion.

acute_crises.vaso_occlusive: Severe bone pain (back, limbs, chest), dactylitis, priapism
acute_crises.acute_chest: Fever + chest pain + new infiltrate + tachypnoea + hypoxia
acute_crises.splenic_sequestration: Sudden splenomegaly + pallor + shock (rapid pooling of blood)
acute_crises.aplastic_crisis: Severe anaemia + very low reticulocytes (parvovirus B19)

differentials.name: Osteomyelitis
differentials.distinguishing: Localised bony tenderness + fever; Salmonella common in SCD; MRI/bone scan

differentials.name: Septic Arthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Hot, swollen joint; restricted movement; USS/aspiration of joint

differentials.name: Viral Arthritis (parvovirus)
differentials.distinguishing: Symmetrical; slapped-cheek rash; aplastic crisis concurrent

differentials.name: Pneumonia
differentials.distinguishing: Consolidation without infarction; ACS can mimic and coexist

differentials.name: Acute Abdomen
differentials.distinguishing: Mesenteric sickling can mimic appendicitis; USS, surgical review

topic:hiv_child.name: Paediatric HIV Infection
topic:hiv_child.overview: Nigeria has the second highest burden of children living with HIV globally. Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) accounts for >90% of paediatric HIV. Untreated, 50% of perinatally infected infants die before age 2. Early infant diagnosis (EID) and early ART are transformative. Presentation may be nonspecific — maintain high index of suspicion.

pearls.hpc_onset: Perinatally infected infants may present at any age. Three patterns: (1) Early progressors — severe disease in first year (AIDS-defining illness); (2) Moderate progressors — symptomatic by age 5; (3) Long-term non-progressors — may remain asymptomatic for years. Ask about maternal HIV status, ANC attendance, PMTCT uptake.
pearls.hpc_character: Recurrent bacterial infections, failure to thrive, chronic diarrhoea, persistent oral candidiasis, lymphadenopathy, and parotid gland enlargement are the cardinal features of paediatric HIV. Any child with recurrent serious bacterial infections = test for HIV.
pearls.sr_fever: HIV-associated fever: opportunistic infections. Common in Nigeria: TB (most common OI), PCP pneumonia (Pneumocystis jirovecii — hypoxic pneumonia without chest signs), cryptosporidium diarrhoea, disseminated fungal infections (cryptococcal meningitis), CMV, HSV.
pearls.exam_general: WHO HIV staging: Stage 1 (asymptomatic/lymphadenopathy) → Stage 2 (minor conditions — oral candidiasis, recurrent URTI) → Stage 3 (severe conditions — severe pneumonia, chronic diarrhoea, TB) → Stage 4 (AIDS-defining — PCP, cryptococcosis, disseminated CMV, wasting syndrome).
pearls.exam_chest: PCP pneumonia (Pneumocystis jirovecii): presents at 3–6 months of age. Severe hypoxia (SpO₂ may be <70%) with minimal chest signs — this disparity is characteristic. CXR: bilateral perihilar ground-glass infiltrates. Treat with high-dose co-trimoxazole.
pearls.ix_fbc: HIV testing: Infants <18 months — HIV DNA PCR (not antibody tests — maternal antibodies cross placenta). Children >18 months — HIV rapid antibody test (confirm with second test). CD4 count: absolute number and CD4% (percentage more useful in young children). CD4% <25% = significant immunosuppression.
pearls.meds_general: ART: all HIV-positive children should receive ART regardless of CD4 or WHO stage (treat-all policy). First-line: ABC + 3TC + DTG (>4 weeks, dolutegravir). Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis: all HIV-positive children from 6 weeks. Isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT): 6 months in all HIV-positive children without active TB.
pearls.pmh_general: Nutritional assessment essential — HIV wasting syndrome. Screen for TB at every visit. Monitor growth, developmental milestones, and neurocognitive development. Disclosure of HIV status appropriate by adolescence.

symptoms: Failure to thrive / poor weight gain
Recurrent bacterial infections (pneumonia, sinusitis, otitis media)
Skin conditions (seborrhoeic dermatitis, molluscum, herpes zoster)

differentials.name: Severe Malnutrition (SAM)
differentials.distinguishing: Low MUAC/WHZ; no recurrent infections; HIV test negative; improves with nutrition

differentials.name: Primary Immunodeficiency
differentials.distinguishing: Rare; family history; HIV negative; specialist immunological workup

differentials.name: TB alone
differentials.distinguishing: HIV negative; household TB contact; responds to ATT alone

differentials.name: Lymphoma
differentials.distinguishing: Painless LN; mediastinal mass; biopsy; HIV can coexist — always test

topic:nephrotic_syndrome_child.name: Nephrotic Syndrome — Childhood
topic:nephrotic_syndrome_child.overview: Characterised by the nephrotic tetrad: heavy proteinuria (>40 mg/m²/hour or 3+ on dipstick), hypoalbuminaemia (<25 g/L), oedema, and hyperlipidaemia. Minimal change disease (MCD) accounts for 80% in children aged 1–8 years and is steroid-responsive. Secondary causes: HIV, malaria, hepatitis B, SLE.

pearls.hpc_onset: Peak age: 2–5 years. Parents typically notice progressive eyelid puffiness (first in morning), then ankle swelling, then generalised oedema. Ascites and scrotal/labial oedema in severe cases. Ask about preceding throat infection (post-streptococcal vs nephritic syndrome distinction).
pearls.hpc_character: Frothy urine (proteinuria) is a key symptom — ask specifically. Reduced urine output. Complications: infections (especially S. pneumoniae peritonitis — functional immunoglobulin loss), thromboembolism (loss of anticoagulant proteins), AKI.
pearls.sr_urinary: Urine dipstick: 3+ or 4+ protein on dipstick = significant proteinuria. Urine protein:creatinine ratio >200 mg/mmol = nephrotic range. Haematuria if haematuria present suggests nephritic component or secondary cause.
pearls.exam_general: Bilateral pitting oedema: periorbital (most visible in morning), pedal, ascites, pleural effusions, scrotal/labial oedema. Malnutrition from protein loss. Look for Cushingoid features (previous steroid treatment).
pearls.ix_fbc: Urine microscopy: lipid-laden oval fat bodies, fatty casts. 24-hour urine protein OR spot protein:creatinine ratio. Serum albumin (<25 g/L = nephrotic). Lipid profile: hypercholesterolaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia. Complement (C3, C4): low in membranoproliferative GN, lupus nephritis.
pearls.ix_lft: Renal biopsy: NOT routine in first presentation of childhood nephrotic syndrome aged 1–8 years (presumed MCD — start steroids). Biopsy indicated: age <1 or >8 years, haematuria, hypertension, low C3, steroid-resistant, family history.
pearls.pmh_general: Secondary causes (important in Nigeria): malaria-associated nephropathy (Plasmodium malariae → membranoproliferative GN), HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN — focal segmental GS), hepatitis B membranous nephropathy. Always test HIV, hepatitis B serology.
pearls.meds_general: First-line: prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day (max 60 mg) × 4–6 weeks, then alternate day × 4–6 weeks. 80% of MCD responds to steroids (steroid-sensitive NS). Steroid-resistant (no response in 4 weeks): renal biopsy + consider cyclosporin/tacrolimus. Albumin infusion + frusemide for resistant oedema. Penicillin V prophylaxis during active nephrosis.

investigations.key_findings: Hypoalbuminaemia + massive proteinuria + oedema = nephrotic syndrome. Low C3 = secondary cause (MPGN, lupus, post-strep). Normal C3 + age 1–8 = MCD (respond to steroids).

differentials.name: Nephritic Syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Haematuria; hypertension; oliguria; RBC casts; less proteinuria; low C3

differentials.name: Severe Malnutrition
differentials.distinguishing: Low MUAC/albumin; no proteinuria on dipstick; no hyperlipidaemia

differentials.name: Heart Failure
differentials.distinguishing: Raised JVP; gallop rhythm; CXR cardiomegaly; BNP elevated

differentials.name: Liver Failure
differentials.distinguishing: Jaundice; coagulopathy; very elevated liver enzymes; cirrhosis on USS

differentials.name: Hypothyroidism
differentials.distinguishing: Goitre; dry skin; constipation; TSH elevated; puffiness without true pitting

topic:asthma_child.name: Childhood Asthma — Acute Exacerbation
topic:asthma_child.overview: Chronic inflammatory airway disease characterised by variable airflow obstruction and bronchial hyperresponsiveness. Prevalence increasing in Nigerian cities. Triggers: viral URTI (most common), allergens (dust mites, cockroach, cat, dog), exercise, cold air, smoke. BTS/SIGN severity classification guides treatment.

pearls.hpc_triggers: Identify the trigger — viral URTI (most common in children), allergen exposure (house dust mite, cockroach, mould — common in Nigerian homes), exercise, cold air, smoke (active/passive), NSAIDs, beta-blockers. The trigger determines management and prevention.
pearls.hpc_character: Classic triad: wheeze + dyspnoea + chest tightness. Cough-variant asthma: chronic nocturnal cough without wheeze (often misdiagnosed as URTI). Ask: Does it come and go? Does it wake from sleep? Response to salbutamol (reliever)?
pearls.sr_fever: Fever usually indicates viral trigger (URTI). High fever suggests bacterial co-infection. Beta-blockers contraindicated — remind yourself on every case. NSAIDs can precipitate asthma in sensitised individuals (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease).
pearls.exam_chest: BTS severity: Mild — PEFR >75%, no accessory muscle use. Moderate — PEFR 50–75%, some accessory muscle use. Severe — PEFR 33–50%, can't complete sentences, tachycardia, accessory muscle use. Life-threatening — PEFR <33%, silent chest (NO wheeze = no airflow), SpO₂ <92%, exhaustion, cyanosis, altered consciousness.
pearls.ix_pefr: PEFR % predicted: age + height-based nomogram. <50% = severe; <33% = life-threatening. PEFR before and 20 min after bronchodilator documents reversibility (>15% improvement = significant bronchodilator response). Inability to perform PEFR = severe episode.
pearls.ix_abg: ABG in severe/life-threatening asthma: initially hypocapnia (PaCO₂ low — hyperventilation). NORMAL or RISING PaCO₂ in severe asthma = RESPIRATORY MUSCLE FATIGUE = PRE-ARREST SIGN. Escalate immediately. Never sedate in acute asthma — can precipitate apnoea.
pearls.meds_general: Acute: SABA (salbutamol 2.5–5 mg nebulised every 20 min × 3, then PRN). Add ipratropium bromide (250 mcg nebulised) in moderate-severe. Systemic corticosteroids: prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg (max 40 mg) × 3–5 days. Oxygen (high-flow). IV magnesium sulphate (25–40 mg/kg) for severe/life-threatening. ICU/intubation if deteriorating.
pearls.pmh_general: Previous ICU admission, intubation, or >2 hospital admissions in a year = high-risk asthma. Sensitisers in history: atopy (eczema, allergic rhinitis, food allergy). Family history of atopy. Non-compliance with preventer (ICS) is the most common reason for exacerbations.

signs_by_severity.mild: PEFR >75%, talking in sentences, mild tachycardia
signs_by_severity.moderate: PEFR 50–75%, speaking in phrases, accessory muscle use, SpO₂ >92%
signs_by_severity.severe: PEFR 33–50%, speaking words only, marked accessory use, SpO₂ <92%, HR >125, RR >30
signs_by_severity.life_threatening: PEFR <33%, silent chest, SpO₂ <92%, bradycardia, exhaustion, cyanosis, altered consciousness

differentials.name: Bronchiolitis
differentials.distinguishing: Age <2 years; RSV; first episode wheeze; hyperinflation; no response to salbutamol

differentials.name: Foreign Body Aspiration
differentials.distinguishing: Unilateral wheeze; sudden onset; choking history; asymmetric CXR

differentials.name: Croup
differentials.distinguishing: Stridor (not wheeze); barking cough; no lower airway signs

differentials.name: Cardiac Failure
differentials.distinguishing: Cardiac history; S3 gallop; CXR cardiomegaly; JVP raised; bilateral crackles

differentials.name: Vocal Cord Dysfunction
differentials.distinguishing: Inspiratory stridor; exercise-induced; normal spirometry between episodes; resolves spontaneously

topic:congenital_heart_disease.name: Congenital Heart Disease
topic:congenital_heart_disease.overview: Structural cardiac abnormalities present from birth. Incidence: ~8 per 1000 live births. Classified as: acyanotic (left-to-right shunts — VSD, ASD, PDA) or cyanotic (right-to-left shunts — Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA, tricuspid atresia). In Nigeria, rheumatic heart disease also remains common.

pearls.hpc_onset: Age of presentation by lesion: (1) Duct-dependent lesions present in first week of life (TGA, pulmonary atresia, critical coarctation) — when ductus closes. (2) VSD/ASD — murmur noted at routine check, or presents with failure to thrive/chest infections at 2–3 months when PVR falls. (3) TOF — cyanosis from birth or worsening cyanosis at 3–6 months.
pearls.hpc_character: Heart failure in infants: poor feeding (fatigues at breast), sweating during feeds, poor weight gain, tachypnoea, recurrent lower respiratory infections. Cyanosis: distinguish central (low SpO₂, blue tongue) from peripheral (blue lips/hands, normal SpO₂ — usually cold or distressed).
pearls.sr_fever: Rheumatic fever: sore throat (Group A Strep) → Jones criteria: major (carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules) + minor (fever, elevated ESR/CRP, prolonged PR interval, previous RF). Carditis in acute RF → mitral regurgitation + later mitral stenosis.
pearls.exam_cardiovascular: Murmur characteristics: VSD — pan-systolic, lower left sternal border. ASD — systolic ejection murmur 2nd left ICS + fixed split S2. PDA — continuous machinery murmur 2nd left ICS. TOF — ejection systolic murmur (pulmonary stenosis), absent P2. Assess: thrill, heaves, S3/S4, JVP, hepatomegaly.
pearls.ix_fbc: Cyanotic CHD: polycythaemia (compensatory — Hct may exceed 70%). Thrombocytopaenia and coagulopathy from polycythaemia. Hyperuricaemia. FBC + renal profile in all CHD before surgery.
pearls.ix_ecg: ECG findings: Right ventricular hypertrophy (TOF — right axis deviation, R>S in V1). Left ventricular hypertrophy (large VSD, AS — deep S V1, tall R V5/V6). Biventricular hypertrophy (large VSD with pulmonary hypertension). Prolonged PR = 1st degree AV block (rheumatic fever).
pearls.ix_cxr: CXR: Boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot) = TOF (small pulmonary artery + RVH + oligaemic lung fields). Egg-on-side heart (TGA — narrow superior mediastinum). Cardiomegaly + plethoric lung fields = large VSD/PDA/ASD. Cardiomegaly + pulmonary oedema = LV failure.
pearls.meds_general: PGE1 (prostaglandin E1) — maintains ductal patency in duct-dependent lesions (while awaiting surgery). Heart failure: frusemide + captopril. TOF spell (hypercyanotic): knee-chest position, oxygen, IV morphine, beta-blockers (propranolol). Rheumatic fever: benzathine penicillin G monthly for secondary prophylaxis.

common_lesions.vsd: Most common CHD (30%). Pan-systolic murmur LLSB. Small = self-closing. Large = failure to thrive, pulmonary hypertension, Eisenmenger's.
common_lesions.asd: Secundum most common. Systolic ejection murmur + fixed split S2. Often asymptomatic in childhood.
common_lesions.pda: Continuous machinery murmur. Premature infants: indomethacin/ibuprofen to close. Full-term: surgical/transcatheter ligation.
common_lesions.tof: Tetralogy: PS + VSD + overriding aorta + RVH. Boot heart on CXR. Hypercyanotic spells. Surgical repair at 3–6 months.
common_lesions.tga: Cyanosis from birth. Egg-on-side heart. Urgent balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure). Arterial switch operation within first 2 weeks.

differentials.name: Respiratory Distress Syndrome (neonate)
differentials.distinguishing: Prematurity; no murmur; CXR: ground-glass; no ductal dependency

differentials.name: Sepsis (neonate)
differentials.distinguishing: No murmur; blood culture positive; responds to antibiotics

differentials.name: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension
differentials.distinguishing: Perinatal asphyxia/meconium; ECHO shows suprasystemic PA pressure; no structural lesion

differentials.name: Anaemia
differentials.distinguishing: Flow murmur; no fixed split; responds to iron; echocardiography normal

topic:rickets.name: Nutritional Rickets
topic:rickets.overview: Failure of mineralisation of growing bone cartilage and osteoid. Most common cause in Nigeria: Vitamin D deficiency (inadequate sunlight + diet) and calcium-deficiency rickets (dietary calcium deficiency without Vitamin D deficiency — specific to Africa/Nigeria). Age: 3 months to 3 years (peak growing period).

pearls.hpc_onset: Ask about: breastfeeding duration (breast milk low in Vitamin D), sun exposure (swaddling practices, staying indoors), diet (calcium-rich foods, fish), delayed walking/motor milestones (bone pain and weakness), recurrent fractures.
pearls.hpc_character: Early: irritability, sweating on head (cranial sweating). Later: bony deformities — bowing of legs, beading of ribs ('rachitic rosary'), wrist and ankle swelling (cupping of metaphyses), Harrison's sulcus (costal indentation at diaphragm level), frontal bossing, delayed fontanelle closure.
pearls.exam_general: Specific signs: Rachitic rosary (palpable knobby swellings at costochondral junctions along ribs). Harrison's sulcus (horizontal groove above costal margin). Craniotabes (ping-pong ball skull in infants — yielding of skull on pressure). Wrist swelling (cupping). Genu varum (bow legs) or genu valgum (knock knees).
pearls.ix_fbc: Classic biochemistry: low/normal serum calcium, low/normal phosphate, MARKEDLY elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP), elevated PTH, low/normal Vitamin D (25-OH-D3). In calcium-deficiency rickets: serum calcium low or normal, Vitamin D may be normal — ALP is the most sensitive marker.
pearls.ix_cxr: Wrist X-ray (gold standard for diagnosis): widened, irregular, frayed, cupped metaphyses ('fraying and cupping'). Loss of zone of provisional calcification. Long bone bowing. Looser zones (pseudo-fractures) in severe cases. Skull X-ray: delayed suture closure, frontal bossing.
pearls.meds_general: Treatment: Vitamin D₂ or D₃ (stoss therapy or daily dosing). High-dose stoss: 150,000–600,000 IU oral single dose. Daily: 1000–5000 IU/day × 3 months then maintenance. Calcium supplements (calcium-deficiency rickets). Sun exposure counselling. Diet: oily fish, eggs, fortified foods.

differentials.name: Physiological Bow Legs
differentials.distinguishing: Normal biochemistry; normal X-ray; resolves spontaneously by age 2

differentials.name: Blount's Disease
differentials.distinguishing: Unilateral/asymmetric; X-ray: beaking of medial proximal tibial metaphysis; no biochemistry changes

differentials.name: Hypophosphataemic Rickets (X-linked)
differentials.distinguishing: Low phosphate; normal Vitamin D; normal calcium; positive family history (X-linked dominant)

differentials.name: Vitamin D-dependent Rickets
differentials.distinguishing: Genetic; Vitamin D supplementation doesn't fully correct; specialist referral

topic:bronchiolitis.name: Bronchiolitis
topic:bronchiolitis.overview: Acute viral lower respiratory tract infection of infants, affecting bronchioles. Most common cause: RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus) — 70–80%. Others: rhinovirus, parainfluenza, adenovirus, metapneumovirus. Peak incidence: 2–6 months. Epidemic in rainy/harmattan season.

pearls.hpc_onset: Typically: 2–3 day prodrome (URTI — coryza, low-grade fever) then worsening respiratory symptoms. Peak severity at days 3–5. Resolves in 7–14 days (wheeze may persist). Risk factors for severe disease: age <3 months, prematurity (<35 weeks), congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease, immunocompromise.
pearls.hpc_character: Wheeze + fine crackles + tachypnoea + hyperinflation in an infant during respiratory illness season = bronchiolitis. Key: this is the FIRST episode of wheeze — if recurrent, consider asthma. No salbutamol response (bronchiolitis is not asthma — small airway obstruction from mucus plugs and inflammation, not bronchospasm).
pearls.exam_chest: Hyperinflation (barrel chest in infants). Subcostal and intercostal recession. Fine inspiratory crackles AND expiratory wheeze (both present). Prolonged expiratory phase. In severe cases: head bobbing, nasal flaring, grunting, central cyanosis, apnoeas (especially in young infants <3 months).
pearls.ix_fbc: Clinical diagnosis — investigations rarely needed. CXR if severe or diagnostic uncertainty: hyperinflation (>6 posterior ribs), areas of atelectasis (partial collapse — right upper lobe common), perihilar shadowing. No antibiotics (viral cause). Nasopharyngeal aspirate: RSV antigen/PCR if needed for infection control.
pearls.meds_general: Supportive treatment ONLY: oxygen (goal SpO₂ ≥92%), NG feeds or IV fluids if unable to feed, nasal suction (isotonic saline + suction). DO NOT give: salbutamol (no evidence), ipratropium, corticosteroids, antibiotics, adrenaline (controversial), ribavirin (only severe immunocompromised). High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) for moderate-severe disease — reduces intubation rate.

differentials.name: Asthma
differentials.distinguishing: Age >12–18 months; recurrent wheeze; responds to salbutamol; family history; no viral prodrome

differentials.name: Pneumonia
differentials.distinguishing: High fever; consolidation on CXR; WBC elevated; responds to antibiotics

differentials.name: Foreign Body Aspiration
differentials.distinguishing: Sudden onset; unilateral wheeze; choking history; asymmetric CXR

differentials.name: Croup
differentials.distinguishing: Inspiratory stridor; barking cough; no wheeze or crackles; subglottic narrowing on CXR (steeple sign)

topic:intussusception.name: Intussusception
topic:intussusception.overview: Telescoping of one segment of bowel into an adjacent segment, causing bowel obstruction and ischaemia. Most common in infants aged 3 months to 3 years. Ileocolic junction is the most common site. In older children, a lead point (Meckel's diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma, HSP) is more likely.

pearls.hpc_onset: Classic intermittent colicky abdominal pain — infant draws legs up to chest, screams, then appears completely normal between episodes (30–60 min interval). Parents may describe the child as having 'episodes of pain' with periods of normal activity in between.
pearls.hpc_character: Later: vomiting becomes bile-stained. 'Red-currant jelly' stool (blood + mucus from bowel ischaemia) — classic but late sign (present in only 50%, indicates ischaemia). Passing this sign to examiner is key. Lethargy (from pain + dehydration).
pearls.exam_abdomen: Sausage-shaped mass in right upper quadrant or along the line of the colon (Dance's sign = empty right iliac fossa as the caecum telescopes inward). Rectal examination: blood on glove. Peritonism (guarding, rebound) = perforation — urgent surgery.
pearls.ix_fbc: Abdominal USS (diagnostic investigation of choice): 'target sign' (bull's-eye) on transverse view — concentric rings of telescoped bowel. 'Pseudokidney sign' on longitudinal view. Sensitivity ~97%, specificity ~100%. Plain AXR: signs of bowel obstruction, soft tissue mass, absence of bowel gas in RIF.
pearls.meds_general: Non-operative reduction (if no peritonism, viable bowel, <48h history): air enema reduction (pneumatic) under fluoroscopy or USS guidance — success rate 70–90%. Surgical reduction if: enema fails, peritonitis, perforation, prolonged history, no air in rectum. IV access + fluid resuscitation before any procedure.

symptoms: Legs drawn up to chest during pain

differentials.name: Gastroenteritis
differentials.distinguishing: Diarrhoea from onset; no sausage mass; USS normal; no red-currant jelly

differentials.name: Malrotation with Volvulus
differentials.distinguishing: Bilious vomiting; X-ray: duodenal obstruction; double-bubble; UGI contrast urgent

differentials.name: Meckel's Diverticulitis
differentials.distinguishing: No sausage mass; can be lead point for intussusception; Meckel's scan

differentials.name: Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP)
differentials.distinguishing: Palpable purpura; arthritis; haematuria; can cause intussusception as lead point

differentials.name: Incarcerated Hernia
differentials.distinguishing: Inguinal/umbilical hernia; non-reducible; USS/clinically differentiated

topic:croup.name: Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis)
topic:croup.overview: Viral infection causing subglottic airway oedema — presents with the classic triad of barking cough + inspiratory stridor + hoarse voice. Most common cause: parainfluenza virus type 1. Peak age: 6 months to 3 years. Occurs in epidemics. Most cases are mild and self-limiting.

pearls.hpc_onset: Typically preceded by 1–2 days of URTI (runny nose, low-grade fever). Symptoms are worst at night — child wakes with barking (seal-like) cough and inspiratory stridor. Parent may describe sounding like a 'barking dog' or 'foghorn'.
pearls.hpc_character: Severity varies: mild (barking cough + stridor only when crying/agitated) → moderate (stridor at rest + recession) → severe (stridor + cyanosis + exhaustion). Do NOT agitate the child (worsening stridor) — assess calmly. Spasmodic croup: recurrent, afebrile, allergic component.
pearls.exam_chest: Westley croup score: stridor (0–2) + retractions (0–3) + air entry (0–2) + cyanosis (0–4) + consciousness (0–5). Score >8 = severe. Stethoscope: inspiratory stridor transmitted throughout chest. No wheeze (distinguishes from asthma). Avoid direct laryngoscopy — risk of causing complete obstruction.
pearls.ix_cxr: Steeple sign on AP CXR (subglottic narrowing — pencil-shaped trachea). Classic but present in only 50%. Neck X-ray: steeple sign more obvious. Investigations rarely needed in typical croup — clinical diagnosis.
pearls.meds_general: Mild: oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (single dose) — reduces hospitalisation, croup score, and stridor duration. Moderate-severe: nebulised adrenaline (l-adrenaline 1 mg/mL, 5 mL) for immediate relief — onset 10 min, lasts 2h (observe for rebound for 3–4h). High-flow O₂ + mist (limited evidence). Intubation (nasotracheal, one size smaller) for severe obstruction.

signs: Inspiratory stridor (mild: only with agitation; severe: at rest)

differentials.name: Epiglottitis
differentials.distinguishing: HIGH fever (>39°C); toxic appearance; drooling; no barking cough; tripod posture; DO NOT examine throat

differentials.name: Foreign Body Aspiration
differentials.distinguishing: Sudden onset; no fever; no coryzal prodrome; asymmetric wheeze or stridor; CXR/bronchoscopy

differentials.name: Bacterial Tracheitis
differentials.distinguishing: High fever; toxic; not relieved by adrenaline; requires intubation; WBC very high

differentials.name: Anaphylaxis
differentials.distinguishing: Urticaria; angioedema; sudden onset; allergen exposure; adrenaline response

differentials.name: Retropharyngeal Abscess
differentials.distinguishing: Fever; neck stiffness; drooling; difficulty swallowing; soft-tissue neck X-ray

topic:cerebral_palsy.name: Cerebral Palsy
topic:cerebral_palsy.overview: Group of permanent, non-progressive disorders of movement and posture, caused by damage to the developing brain (before, during, or after birth, up to age 2–3 years). Commonest cause of physical disability in childhood. In Nigeria, major risk factors: birth asphyxia (most common), neonatal sepsis, neonatal jaundice (kernicterus), cerebral malaria, prematurity, TBI.

pearls.hpc_onset: Key history: perinatal history (birth at home/hospital, prolonged labour, fetal distress, Apgar scores, resuscitation needed), neonatal jaundice (kernicterus — athetoid CP), neonatal seizures, meningitis, malaria with prolonged coma. Developmental delay is often the presenting complaint — parents notice child isn't reaching milestones.
pearls.hpc_character: Motor delay: not sitting by 9 months, not walking by 18 months. Abnormal gait (scissor gait, toe walking, hemiplegic gait). Abnormal tone: hypotonia early (floppy baby) → spasticity later. Primitive reflexes persisting beyond expected age. Associated features: intellectual disability (50%), epilepsy (25–35%), visual impairment, hearing loss, speech and language delay.
pearls.exam_neuro: Classify by motor type: Spastic (85%) — increased tone, brisk reflexes, clonus, Babinski sign. Dyskinetic/Athetoid (10%) — involuntary movements (athetosis, chorea, dystonia) — associated with kernicterus. Ataxic (5%) — cerebellar signs, poor coordination, intention tremor. Classify by distribution: hemiplegia, diplegia (legs more than arms — prematurity), quadriplegia (most severe), monoplegia.
pearls.ix_fbc: MRI brain (investigation of choice): identifies structural lesion (periventricular leucomalacia — prematurity, cortical atrophy — hypoxia, basal ganglia lesion — kernicterus/hypoxia, other structural malformation). TORCH screen (if congenital infection suspected). Metabolic screen (exclude treatable causes). EEG if seizures suspected.
pearls.pmh_general: Comorbidities to assess at every visit: epilepsy (dose and seizure control), vision (squint, refractive error), hearing (sensorineural loss), nutrition/feeding difficulties (GORD, dysphagia, aspiration), scoliosis, hip subluxation/dislocation (all spastic CP), contractures, dental health, cognitive function.
pearls.meds_general: MDT approach: physiotherapy (prevents contractures, improves function), occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, orthotics (AFO, KAFO). Spasticity: oral baclofen, tizanidine, intrathecal baclofen pump, botulinum toxin A (local muscle relaxation). Orthopaedic surgery (selective dorsal rhizotomy, hip reconstruction). Antiepileptics for seizures.

differentials.name: Progressive Neurological Disorder
differentials.distinguishing: CP is NON-PROGRESSIVE — if the child is deteriorating, consider neurodegenerative disease (leukodystrophy, neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis)

differentials.name: Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA)
differentials.distinguishing: Flaccid weakness; tongue fasciculations; no upper motor neuron signs; SMN gene test

differentials.name: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
differentials.distinguishing: Male; Gowers' sign; calf pseudohypertrophy; creatine kinase very high; gene test

differentials.name: Global Developmental Delay
differentials.distinguishing: May have normal tone; multiple developmental domains affected; cause may overlap with CP

topic:dengue_fever.name: Dengue Fever
topic:dengue_fever.overview: Arboviral infection (flavivirus, serotypes 1–4) transmitted by Aedes aegypti mosquito. Increasingly common in Nigerian cities. Key danger: dengue haemorrhagic fever (DHF) and dengue shock syndrome (DSS) in secondary infections. Critical phase: around day 3–5 when fever breaks and plasma leakage begins.

pearls.hpc_onset: Incubation: 4–10 days post-mosquito bite. Sudden onset of high fever. Classic: 'breakbone fever' — severe myalgia/arthralgia ('bones breaking feeling'). Biphasic fever (saddle-back fever) in some cases.
pearls.sr_fever: Warning signs of severe dengue (days 3–5, as fever breaks): abdominal pain/tenderness, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation (pleural effusion, ascites), mucosal bleeding, lethargy/restlessness, liver enlargement >2 cm, rising Hct with rapid drop in platelet count.
pearls.exam_skin: Rash: flushed face early; then maculopapular or morbilliform rash 3–5 days (trunk → spreads centrifugally) with 'islands of white' (sparing). Petechiae on lower limbs. Tourniquet test (Rumpel-Leede): inflate BP cuff to midpoint between systolic and diastolic for 5 minutes — ≥10 petechiae per square inch = positive.
pearls.ix_fbc: Key findings: thrombocytopaenia (platelets <100 × 10⁹/L, may fall to <20). Rising haematocrit (Hct) ≥20% above baseline = plasma leakage (critical sign). Leucopaenia (WBC <5 × 10⁹/L). NS1 antigen (days 1–5): highly sensitive and specific. IgM/IgG antibodies (from day 5).
pearls.meds_general: No antiviral treatment. Dengue fever: paracetamol (NOT NSAIDs — bleeding risk, NOT aspirin — Reye's syndrome). Ensure adequate oral fluid intake. DHF/severe: IV crystalloids carefully (avoid overhydration — plasma is leaking, not deficient). Blood transfusion/platelet transfusion only for active haemorrhage. Monitor Hct 4-hourly in severe cases.

differentials.name: Malaria
differentials.distinguishing: Positive blood film/RDT; no tourniquet test; different fever pattern; endemic area

differentials.name: Typhoid
differentials.distinguishing: Stepwise fever; relative bradycardia; blood culture; leucopaenia + lymphocytosis

differentials.name: Measles
differentials.distinguishing: Koplik spots; coryzal prodrome; characteristic rash (cranio-caudal); no thrombocytopaenia

differentials.name: Leptospirosis
differentials.distinguishing: Water exposure; conjunctival suffusion; jaundice; renal failure; Leptospira serology

topic:urinary_tract_infection_child.name: Urinary Tract Infection — Childhood
topic:urinary_tract_infection_child.overview: Common bacterial infection. Girls > Boys (except neonatal period where boys predominate). Most common organism: E. coli (75–85%). Vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) is a key predisposing factor — UTI in young children requires investigation for structural abnormality. Renal scarring from recurrent pyelonephritis is a long-term risk.

pearls.hpc_onset: Presentation varies by age: Neonates/infants: nonspecific — poor feeding, fever without focus, jaundice, vomiting. Toddlers: fever, vomiting, abdominal pain, smelly urine. Older children: classic — dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, haematuria (lower UTI), + fever/loin pain/rigors (upper UTI/pyelonephritis).
pearls.sr_fever: Fever >38°C without source in infants/toddlers = consider UTI. Urine microscopy/culture is mandatory in febrile infants <3 months. High fever + rigors + loin pain/tenderness = pyelonephritis (upper UTI) — systemic treatment.
pearls.sr_urinary: Ask specifically: dysuria, frequency, urgency, smelly urine, haematuria, wetting/incontinence (regression in a toilet-trained child). In infants: enquire about urine stream (poor stream in boys = posterior urethral valves).
pearls.ix_fbc: Urinalysis: dipstick positive for nitrites (bacteria converting nitrates) AND leucocyte esterase (WBCs) = high probability of UTI. Nitrites alone: sensitive (~50%) but specific. Leucocytes alone: less specific. Send MSSU (midstream clean-catch) for microscopy and culture. Suprapubic aspiration in infants. Colony count ≥100,000 CFU/mL = significant growth.
pearls.ix_lft: Pyelonephritis: elevated CRP + WBC (neutrophilia). Blood culture if <3 months or systemically unwell. Imaging: renal USS (all first UTI <2 years — structural anomalies). DMSA scan (4–6 months post-UTI — renal scarring). MAG3/DTPA (VUR — micturating cystourethrogram in selected cases).
pearls.meds_general: Lower UTI: oral trimethoprim (5–7 days) or nitrofurantoin (5–7 days). Pyelonephritis: IV ceftriaxone or gentamicin (if <3 months or vomiting/systemically unwell) → step-down to oral when tolerating. Duration: 7–10 days for upper UTI. Prophylaxis: cotrimoxazole/nitrofurantoin for recurrent UTI or VUR while awaiting imaging. Circumcision reduces UTI risk in boys with recurrent infections.

by_age.neonates_infants: Fever without focus, poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, irritability
by_age.toddlers: Fever, vomiting, abdominal pain, smelly urine, regression in toilet training
by_age.older_children: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, haematuria (lower), + loin pain + fever (upper)

differentials.name: Vulvovaginitis
differentials.distinguishing: Girls; discharge; dysuria at end of stream; dipstick negative; culture negative

differentials.name: Appendicitis
differentials.distinguishing: RIF pain; rebound; Alvarado score; AXR/USS

differentials.name: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (adolescent girls)
differentials.distinguishing: Sexually active; vaginal discharge; cervical motion tenderness; gonorrhoea/chlamydia

differentials.name: Viral Cystitis (adenovirus)
differentials.distinguishing: Haematuria; negative culture; USS normal; self-limiting

topic:epilepsy_child.name: Epilepsy — Childhood
topic:epilepsy_child.overview: Epilepsy = ≥2 unprovoked seizures >24 hours apart, OR one unprovoked seizure with high recurrence risk. Affects ~1% of children. In Nigeria: important causes include neonatal hypoxia, meningitis, cerebral malaria, neurocysticercosis, structural brain malformations. Syndromes include childhood absence epilepsy, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, Dravet syndrome, BECTS.

pearls.hpc_onset: Detailed seizure description from witness is essential: Was the child conscious? Eyes open or closed? Limb movements (bilateral or one-sided)? Duration? Post-ictal state (confusion, sleep, focal weakness)? Precipitants: sleep deprivation, fever, flashing lights (photosensitive epilepsy), missed medication.
pearls.hpc_character: Classify seizure type: Focal (one hemisphere — with or without awareness impairment, with or without secondary generalisation). Generalised (both hemispheres — tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic, atonic/drop attacks, tonic). Absence seizures: brief (<20s) staring episodes with eye flickering, no post-ictal state — often misdiagnosed as daydreaming.
pearls.sr_seizures: Duration of seizure is critical: >5 minutes = treat as status epilepticus. Cluster of seizures = high-risk. Postictal deficit >1 hour (Todd's paresis, aphasia) = focal onset, structural cause more likely. Always exclude provoking causes: hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, hyponatraemia, fever, metabolic.
pearls.exam_neuro: Full neurological examination. Look for: neurocutaneous stigmata (ash-leaf spots/café-au-lait — tuberous sclerosis; port-wine stain — Sturge-Weber; axillary freckling — NF1). Head circumference (micro/macrocephaly). Fundoscopy (papilloedema, chorioretinitis). Focal deficits (hemiparesis, visual field defect).
pearls.ix_fbc: EEG: essential for syndrome classification (not diagnosis of epilepsy — EEG may be normal between episodes). MRI brain (preferred over CT — better grey-white differentiation, no radiation): structural cause (tumour, cortical dysplasia, mesial temporal sclerosis, neurocysticercosis). Metabolic screen: glucose, calcium, sodium, magnesium, ammonia (neonatal). Genetic testing (specific syndromes).
pearls.meds_general: First-line by seizure type: Generalised tonic-clonic: sodium valproate or levetiracetam. Absence: ethosuximide or valproate. Focal: carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine. Avoid sodium valproate in girls/women of childbearing age (teratogenic). Status epilepticus: IV diazepam → IV lorazepam → IV phenobarbitone → IV phenytoin → ICU (propofol/thiopentone/midazolam infusion). Drug levels (phenobarbitone, phenytoin, valproate): trough levels to guide dosing.

generalised: Tonic-clonic: rhythmic jerking of all 4 limbs + tongue-biting + incontinence
Absence: brief staring + eye flickering, no post-ictal state
Myoclonic: sudden brief muscle jerks (morning on waking)
Atonic: sudden loss of muscle tone ('drop attacks')
focal: Focal aware: tingling, visual aura, deja vu — preserved consciousness
Focal impaired awareness: automatisms (lip-smacking, hand fumbling), impaired consciousness
Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic: starts focal → generalises

differentials.name: Febrile Seizure
differentials.distinguishing: Age 6mo–5yr; fever >38°C; generalised; brief; normal post-ictally

differentials.name: Syncope (vasovagal)
differentials.distinguishing: Prodrome (dizziness, pallor, visual graying); brief (seconds); upright posture; no post-ictal state

differentials.name: Breath-holding Spells
