differentials.distinguishing: Toddler; precipitated by crying; brief; cyanosis then limpness; no EEG changes

differentials.name: Non-epileptic Attack Disorder (NEAD)
differentials.distinguishing: Adolescent; prolonged; eyes closed; normal EEG during attack; psychological trigger

differentials.name: Hypoglycaemic Seizure
differentials.distinguishing: Glucose <2.2 mmol/L; corrects with dextrose; underlying cause (insulin, SGA, GHD)

topic:rheumatic_fever.name: Acute Rheumatic Fever
topic:rheumatic_fever.overview: Inflammatory disease caused by autoimmune response to Group A Streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis. Peak age: 5–15 years. Rare in <3 and >20 years. Nigeria is a high-burden country for RF and rheumatic heart disease (RHD). Repeated streptococcal attacks cause cumulative valve damage — mitral stenosis is the end result.

pearls.hpc_onset: Latency: 2–4 weeks after GAS pharyngitis (sometimes subclinical sore throat). Always ask about sore throat in the preceding 2–4 weeks. School-age children with migratory joint pain + fever = acute RF until proven otherwise.
pearls.hpc_character: Jones criteria (2015 revision): Major — Carditis (clinical/subclinical on ECHO), Arthritis (polyarthritis in low-risk; monoarthritis/polyarthralgia accepted in high-risk settings like Nigeria), Chorea (Sydenham's), Erythema marginatum, Subcutaneous nodules. Minor — fever, elevated ESR/CRP, prolonged PR interval, arthralgia (only if arthritis NOT a major criterion).
pearls.sr_fever: High fever (38–39°C). Migratory polyarthritis: joints are hot, red, swollen, very tender (disproportionate to findings) — moves from large joint to large joint (knees, ankles, elbows, wrists, hips). Aspirin or NSAIDs cause dramatic relief — ex juvantibus response strongly supports RF.
pearls.exam_cardiovascular: Carditis (50–60% of first episodes): apical pan-systolic murmur (mitral regurgitation — most common). Aortic regurgitation (early diastolic murmur LUSB). Pericarditis — pericardial rub, chest pain. Subclinical carditis (Doppler ECHO shows MR without clinical signs) — important to detect.
pearls.exam_neuro: Sydenham's chorea (10–15%): involuntary, purposeless, rapid movements — especially hands and face. Emotional lability. 'Milking sign' (rhythmic hand squeezing during handshake). Chorea may occur months after the initial episode — isolated late presentation.
pearls.ix_fbc: Evidence of antecedent GAS infection: ASO titre >200 Todd units (or >333 in adults) — elevated in 80%. Anti-DNase B (more sensitive than ASO). Throat culture (positive in only 25–40% of RF). Elevated ESR + CRP. ECG: prolonged PR interval (1st degree AV block) — minor Jones criterion. ECHO (subclinical carditis — mitral regurgitation jets).
pearls.meds_general: Primary: benzathine penicillin G IM 1.2 million units (single dose) — eradicates GAS. Aspirin 50–70 mg/kg/day (anti-inflammatory) for arthritis. Prednisolone for severe carditis (pericarditis, pancarditis). Haloperidol/sodium valproate for chorea. SECONDARY PROPHYLAXIS is critical: benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units IM every 3–4 weeks — prevents recurrent streptococcal infections and cumulative valve damage. Duration: RF without carditis — 5 years or until 21. RF with carditis, no RHD — 10 years or 21. Persistent RHD — 10 years or 40 (whichever longer), sometimes lifelong.

major_jones: Carditis (MR murmur, pericardial rub, cardiac failure)
Erythema marginatum (non-pruritic, migratory, pink, on trunk)
Subcutaneous nodules (over bony prominences — Aschoff nodules)
minor_jones: Arthralgia (only if arthritis not a major criterion)

differentials.name: Reactive Arthritis
differentials.distinguishing: GI or genitourinary infection; asymmetric; may have eye/skin involvement; ASO normal

differentials.name: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA)
differentials.distinguishing: Prolonged >6 weeks; morning stiffness; ANA/RF; no carditis in same pattern

differentials.name: Septic Arthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Monoarticular; very hot, tender; systemic toxicity; joint aspiration — purulent

differentials.name: Infective Endocarditis
differentials.distinguishing: Persisting bacteraemia; embolic phenomena; vegetations on ECHO; blood culture positive

differentials.name: Viral Arthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Non-migratory; ASO normal; viral prodrome; self-limiting

topic:neonatal_jaundice.name: Neonatal Jaundice (Neonatal Hyperbilirubinaemia)
topic:neonatal_jaundice.overview: Jaundice (yellowing of sclera and skin) is detectable when serum bilirubin >85 μmol/L (5 mg/dL). Physiological jaundice: appears day 2–3, peaks day 4–5, resolves by day 10–14. Pathological: appears <24h, rises rapidly, or persists >2 weeks. Kernicterus (bilirubin-induced neurological damage — irreversible) is a preventable cause of cerebral palsy in Nigeria.

pearls.hpc_onset: Onset timing is the most important discriminator: Jaundice at <24 hours = PATHOLOGICAL (haemolysis — ABO/Rh incompatibility, G6PD deficiency). Day 2–5 = physiological or pathological (sepsis, G6PD, haemolysis). >2 weeks = prolonged (breast milk jaundice, hypothyroidism, biliary atresia, neonatal hepatitis).
pearls.hpc_character: Ask about: blood group of mother and baby (ABO/Rh incompatibility — mother O or Rh-negative), family history of jaundice/G6PD deficiency, exposure to naphthalene (mothballs — precipitate G6PD crisis), birth setting, sepsis risk factors.
pearls.sr_fever: Sepsis-associated jaundice: often with temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy. G6PD deficiency: haemolytic jaundice after exposure to oxidant stress (infection, naphthalene, certain drugs — primaquine, nitrofurantoin, dapsone). ABO incompatibility: mother type O, baby type A or B — anti-A or anti-B maternal IgG crosses placenta.
pearls.exam_general: Clinical jaundice assessment (Kramer zones): Zone 1 (face/neck) = bilirubin ~5 mg/dL. Zone 2 (trunk above umbilicus) = ~10. Zone 3 (below umbilicus to knees) = ~15. Zone 4 (knees to ankles) = ~18–20. Zone 5 (palms/soles) = >20. Clinical assessment UNRELIABLE — measure transcutaneous bilirubin (TcB) or serum bilirubin (SBR).
pearls.exam_neuro: Acute bilirubin encephalopathy (ABE): Phase 1 — poor feeding, hypotonia, high-pitched cry. Phase 2 — retrocollis, opisthotonus, fever, shrill cry. Phase 3 — hypotonia, stupor. Kernicterus (chronic): athetoid CP, sensorineural deafness, gaze palsy (upgaze), dental enamel dysplasia.
pearls.ix_fbc: Bilirubin: total and direct (conjugated). SBR plotted on Bhutani nomogram (hour-specific threshold) for phototherapy and exchange transfusion thresholds. Coombs test (DAT): positive = immune-mediated haemolysis (ABO/Rh incompatibility). FBC: anaemia (haemolysis — low Hb + high reticulocytes). G6PD screen (assay or fluorescent spot test). Blood group of mother and baby.
pearls.meds_general: Phototherapy: isomerises bilirubin to non-toxic water-soluble form. Double-surface LED phototherapy most effective. Exchange transfusion: for very high bilirubin, signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy, or failure of phototherapy (double volume exchange = 2 × 85 mL/kg). Maintain hydration. Treat underlying cause (antibiotics for sepsis, etc.).

clinical_features.physiological: Day 2–3 onset; peak day 4–5; resolves by day 14; well-looking infant; SBR within safe zone

causes_by_timing.day_1: Haemolytic disease of newborn (ABO, Rh incompatibility), G6PD deficiency
causes_by_timing.day_2_to_5: Physiological, G6PD, sepsis, polycythaemia, ABO incompatibility
causes_by_timing.week_2_plus: Breast milk jaundice, hypothyroidism, biliary atresia, neonatal hepatitis, G6PD, UTI

differentials.name: Biliary Atresia
differentials.distinguishing: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; pale clay-coloured stools; dark urine; firm liver; USS + HIDA scan; Kasai procedure before 60 days

differentials.name: Neonatal Hepatitis
differentials.distinguishing: Conjugated jaundice; elevated transaminases; TORCH infection; alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency

differentials.name: Hypothyroidism
differentials.distinguishing: Prolonged jaundice; poor feeding; constipation; umbilical hernia; TSH elevated

differentials.name: Polycythaemia
differentials.distinguishing: Hct >65%; plethoric baby; hypoglycaemia; treatment: partial exchange transfusion

topic:kawasaki_disease.name: Kawasaki Disease
topic:kawasaki_disease.overview: Acute self-limiting systemic vasculitis of medium-sized vessels, predominantly affecting children <5 years. The most important complication: coronary artery aneurysms (in 25% if untreated, <5% if treated with IVIG). Aetiology unknown. Diagnosis is clinical — no definitive test. May be underdiagnosed in Nigeria.

pearls.hpc_onset: Classic Kawasaki: fever ≥5 days + ≥4 of 5 principal features (criteria below). Incomplete Kawasaki: fever ≥5 days + only 2–3 features, but ECHO shows coronary abnormalities. Any child with unexplained fever >5 days not responding to antibiotics in a child <5 = consider Kawasaki.
pearls.hpc_character: Fever is HIGH (>39–40°C), remittent, and does NOT respond to antipyretics or antibiotics. The five features (remember: CRASH): Conjunctivitis (bilateral, non-purulent), Rash (polymorphous), Adenopathy (cervical LN >1.5cm), Strawberry tongue / lip changes, Hands/feet (erythema/oedema acutely, then desquamation days 10–14).
pearls.exam_skin: Rash: polymorphous (maculopapular, target-like, urticarial, scarlatiniform). Perianal erythema and early desquamation (early sign). Hands/feet: erythema and firm induration of palms and soles (first week) → periungual desquamation from fingertips outwards (day 10–14 — pathognomonic at this stage).
pearls.exam_cardiovascular: Myocarditis: tachycardia disproportionate to fever. Pericardial effusion. Coronary artery aneurysm (ECHO): left anterior descending or right coronary artery. ECHO at diagnosis, 2 weeks, and 6 weeks. Mitral regurgitation. Gallop rhythm.
pearls.ix_fbc: Elevated inflammatory markers: CRP + ESR markedly raised. FBC: leucocytosis (neutrophilia), anaemia (normocytic), thrombocytosis (>450 × 10⁹/L — second week, characteristic). Sterile pyuria on urine dipstick (urethritis — part of the disease). Elevated ALT (hepatitis — 50%). ECHO: coronary artery diameter > 2.5 SD above mean for body surface area = aneurysm.
pearls.meds_general: IVIG 2 g/kg IV over 10–12 hours (single infusion) — reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25% to <5%. Aspirin: high dose (30–50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses) during febrile phase, then low-dose (3–5 mg/kg/day) for 6–8 weeks (or longer if coronary abnormalities). IVIG resistance (10–15%): second dose IVIG or infliximab. Follow-up cardiology: long-term if coronary aneurysms.

diagnostic_criteria: Changes in lips/oral cavity (strawberry tongue, cracked lips, injected pharynx)
Changes in extremities (erythema/oedema of palms-soles → periungual desquamation)

differentials.name: Viral Exanthem
differentials.distinguishing: Shorter fever; resolves spontaneously; no coronary involvement; specific viral signs

differentials.name: Scarlet Fever
differentials.distinguishing: GAS infection; sandpaper rash; responds to penicillin; ASO elevated

differentials.name: Measles
differentials.distinguishing: Koplik spots; coryza/cough/conjunctivitis triad; not vaccinated; epidemic context

differentials.name: Toxic Shock Syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Staphylococcal/streptococcal toxin; rapid shock; blood culture

differentials.name: Systemic JIA
differentials.distinguishing: Salmon-pink rash; daily fever spikes; arthritis; age >2 years; ferritin very high

topic:henoch_schonlein_purpura.name: Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (IgA Vasculitis)
topic:henoch_schonlein_purpura.overview: Most common systemic vasculitis in children. IgA-mediated small vessel vasculitis affecting skin, joints, gastrointestinal tract, and kidneys. Peak age: 4–7 years. Often triggered by URTI (GAS, viral). Usually self-limiting, but renal involvement (HSP nephritis) is the most serious long-term complication.

pearls.hpc_onset: Tetrad: palpable purpura + arthritis/arthralgia + abdominal pain + renal involvement. NOT all four need to be present simultaneously. Preceded by URTI in 50–75% (1–3 weeks before). Rash is the presenting feature in most cases.
pearls.hpc_character: Palpable purpura: non-blanching (vasculitic), palpable (raised — unlike ITP which is flat), predominantly on lower limbs and buttocks (dependent areas). Abdominal pain (50–70%): colicky, may be severe (mesenteric vasculitis). GI complications: intussusception (HSP is a common lead point in older children), GI haemorrhage.
pearls.exam_skin: Purpuric rash: symmetric distribution on lower limbs (pretibial, ankles) and buttocks. May extend to upper limbs. ALWAYS palpate — must be raised/palpable (distinguishes from thrombocytopaenic purpura). New crops appear over 6–8 weeks.
pearls.sr_urinary: Renal involvement (40%): microscopic haematuria + proteinuria. Check urine dipstick at every visit. Severe nephritis: macroscopic haematuria + nephrotic range proteinuria + hypertension + AKI = poor prognosis. Monthly urine monitoring for 12 months after diagnosis.
pearls.ix_fbc: FBC: platelets NORMAL or elevated (distinguishes from ITP where platelets are low). Elevated IgA (in 50% — not required for diagnosis). Urine dipstick: haematuria + proteinuria = renal involvement. Renal biopsy: if heavy proteinuria or AKI (shows IgA mesangial deposits = IgA nephropathy). ASO titre (preceding GAS infection). Stool occult blood (GI involvement).

tetrad: Palpable purpura (mandatory for diagnosis) — lower limbs and buttocks

differentials.name: ITP (Immune Thrombocytopaenic Purpura)
differentials.distinguishing: Flat (non-palpable) purpura; platelets very low; no arthritis/abdominal pain/renal involvement

differentials.name: Meningococcal Septicaemia
differentials.distinguishing: Toxic appearance; petechiae/purpura spreading rapidly; shock; blood culture positive

differentials.name: Reactive Arthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Arthritis without rash; GI/GU infection preceding; urine normal

differentials.name: SLE
differentials.distinguishing: Butterfly rash; multi-system; ANA/dsDNA positive; older female; complement low

pearl:hpc_onset.content: Always establish exact timing and mode of onset — sudden (vascular, obstructive, haemorrhagic) vs gradual (inflammatory, neoplastic, metabolic) vs intermittent (colic, seizures, arrhythmia). Use 'When exactly did this start? What were you doing at the time? Did it start suddenly or come on slowly?'

pearl:hpc_character.content: Use SOCRATES to characterise any symptom: Site → Onset → Character → Radiation → Associations → Timing/pattern → Exacerbating/relieving factors → Severity (0–10). For pain: distinguish colicky (comes and goes — visceral) from constant (somatic/peritoneal = peritonism).

pearl:exam_general.content: Paediatric general survey: Age-appropriate vital signs first (tachycardia, tachypnoea are the earliest signs of distress). ABCDE approach. Nutritional status (MUAC, weight for age). End-of-bed impression — well, unwell, or critically ill? Colour (pale, jaundiced, cyanosed). Posture and activity level.

pearl:immunisation.content: Nigerian EPI schedule: BCG + OPV-0 (birth), Penta 1/2/3 + OPV 1/2/3 + PCV13 (6/10/14 weeks), IPV (14 weeks), MCV1 + Yellow Fever (9 months), Vitamin A, MCV2 (12–15 months). Always check immunisation card. Unvaccinated child with meningism = cannot exclude Hib/Pneumococcal meningitis on immunisation grounds.

pearl:sr_seizures.content: Seizure description must include: (1) Any warning/aura? (2) Generalised or focal? (3) Exact duration. (4) Consciousness during seizure. (5) Post-ictal state — how long to full recovery? Eyes open = consciousness preserved (focal); Eyes closed with loss of awareness = impaired consciousness. >5 minutes = status epilepticus — treat immediately.

pearl:ix_fbc.content: Interpret FBC systematically: Hb (anaemia — then classify: MCV low=iron def/thal; MCV normal=chronic disease/haemolysis; MCV high=folate/B12) → WBC (neutrophilia=bacterial; lymphocytosis=viral; eosinophilia=parasitic/allergic) → Platelets (low=ITP/DIC/HUS/dengue/SLE; high=Kawasaki/reactive/iron def). Always look at the film (reticulocytes, RBC morphology).

pearl:exam_abdomen.content: Paediatric abdominal examination: Inspect (distension, visible peristalsis, hernias, scars). Observe child's face while palpating — guarding and tenderness better assessed by watching facial expression. Palpate lightly first (superficial tenderness, rigidity) then deeply (organomegaly — start at RIF and work up to liver, then cross to spleen, then kidneys bimanually). Percuss (shifting dullness — ascites; tympany — obstruction). Auscultate last (bowel sounds).

drug:benzathine_penicillin.name: Benzathine Benzylpenicillin G (Bicillin LA)
indications: Primary treatment of GAS pharyngitis (RF prevention)
Secondary prophylaxis of acute rheumatic fever
drug:benzathine_penicillin.dose: 1.2 million units IM single dose (>27 kg) / 600,000 units IM (<27 kg)
drug:benzathine_penicillin.nigerian_pearl: Benzathine penicillin is available at most secondary/tertiary facilities in Nigeria. Monthly injection is preferred over oral penicillin for secondary prophylaxis (better adherence, more reliable protection). Register RF patients in a rheumatic heart disease registry.

drug:iv_artesunate.name: IV Artesunate
indications: Severe malaria (first-line per WHO and FMOH guidelines)
drug:iv_artesunate.dose: 2.4 mg/kg IV at 0h, 12h, 24h, then once daily. Step-down to oral ACT when tolerated.
drug:iv_artesunate.not_quinine: IV artesunate is superior to IV quinine in all RCTs (AQUAMAT trial). Quinine: more side effects (hypoglycaemia, QTc prolongation, cinchonism) — use only when artesunate unavailable.
drug:iv_artesunate.pre_referral: Rectal artesunate 10 mg/kg (single dose) is recommended pre-referral when IV access not available.
drug:iv_artesunate.nigerian_pearl: Artesunate is on Nigeria's essential medicines list. Ensure adequate stock at all levels. Chloroquine is ineffective against P. falciparum in Nigeria — avoid.

drug:vitamin_a.name: Vitamin A Supplementation
drug:vitamin_a.dose: <6 months: 50,000 IU. 6–11 months: 100,000 IU. ≥12 months: 200,000 IU. Repeat on day 2 in measles.
drug:vitamin_a.evidence: Reduces measles mortality by 50%. Reduces mortality from pneumonia and diarrhoea in deficient populations.
drug:vitamin_a.nigerian_pearl: Nigeria has high VAD prevalence, particularly in the north. Vitamin A supplementation is integrated into the EPI schedule (given with MCV1 at 9 months). Measles complicated by corneal ulceration: Vitamin A + tetracycline eye ointment prevent blindness.

guideline:who_malaria_severe.title: WHO Guidelines for Severe Malaria (4th edition, 2022)
key_points: IV artesunate is the first-line treatment for severe malaria in all age groups
Rectal artesunate is recommended as pre-referral treatment when parenteral therapy not available
Blood glucose must be monitored 4-hourly — hypoglycaemia is a medical emergency
Indication for blood transfusion: Hb <5 g/dL with respiratory distress, or Hb <4 g/dL regardless
Corticosteroids are NOT recommended for cerebral malaria (no benefit, potential harm)
LP only after excluding raised ICP; treat as cerebral malaria and do LP later
guideline:who_malaria_severe.nigerian_adaptation: FMOH Nigeria follows WHO guidelines. Artesunate available via NMEP national malaria programme. Avoid: chloroquine (widespread resistance), IM quinine (painful, dangerous). Use phenobarbitone for seizure prophylaxis in cerebral malaria only under specialist guidance.

guideline:imci_classification.title: IMCI — Integrated Management of Childhood Illness
guideline:imci_classification.pearl: IMCI is the core clinical framework for managing sick children in Nigerian primary health facilities. All healthcare workers at PHC level should be IMCI-trained. Respiratory rate count (1 full minute, child calm) is the single most important skill.

guideline:sam_who_10steps.title: WHO 10 Steps for Management of Severe Acute Malnutrition
steps: 1. Treat/prevent HYPOGLYCAEMIA — check BGL immediately, give 10% dextrose 5mL/kg if <3 mmol/L
2. Treat/prevent HYPOTHERMIA — dress child warmly, skin-to-skin, warm room
3. Treat/prevent DEHYDRATION — use ReSoMal (not standard ORS — lower sodium, higher potassium) 5 mL/kg every 30 min × 2h
4. Correct ELECTROLYTE imbalance — potassium, magnesium supplementation
5. Treat/prevent INFECTION — amoxicillin (uncomplicated) or ampicillin + gentamicin (complicated) routinely even without obvious infection
6. Correct MICRONUTRIENT deficiencies — folic acid day 1, then multivitamins + zinc + copper from day 2
7. Begin CAUTIOUS REFEEDING with F-75 (75 kcal/100mL) — 100 kcal/kg/day, 130mL/kg/day
8. Achieve CATCH-UP GROWTH with F-100 or RUTF — 150–220 kcal/kg/day
9. Provide SENSORY STIMULATION — structured play, emotional nurturing
10. PREPARE FOR DISCHARGE — target: weight gain 5g/kg/day × 3 days; MUAC ≥12.5cm; oedema resolved; eating well; no infection

topic:type1_diabetes_child.name: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus — Childhood
topic:type1_diabetes_child.overview: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing absolute insulin deficiency. Most common endocrine disorder in children. Peak age of diagnosis: 5–7 years and early adolescence. Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is the most serious acute complication and is often the mode of presentation in Nigeria where diagnosis is delayed.

pearls.hpc_onset: Classic triad of polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss over weeks. Children may present acutely in DKA — vomiting, abdominal pain, altered consciousness, Kussmaul breathing (deep, sighing respirations — respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis). Ask: excessive thirst, frequent urination, bed-wetting in a previously dry child, weight loss despite eating well.
pearls.hpc_character: DKA diagnostic criteria: hyperglycaemia (BGL >11 mmol/L), ketonaemia/ketonuria, metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L). Severity: Mild (pH 7.2–7.3), Moderate (pH 7.1–7.2), Severe (<7.1). Cerebral oedema is the most feared complication — occurs during treatment, not at presentation.
pearls.sr_fever: Infection is a common precipitant of DKA (raises counter-regulatory hormones). Also: missed insulin doses, new diagnosis. Always look for infection focus in DKA. Fever + DKA = aggressive infection screen.
pearls.exam_general: DKA: Kussmaul breathing (deep, sighing, compensatory), ketotic breath (fruity/acetone smell), dehydration (dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor), tachycardia, hypotension (severe dehydration), altered consciousness (GCS <13 = severe DKA).
pearls.ix_fbc: Bedside: blood glucose (>11 mmol/L), ketones (urine dipstick or blood ketones >3 mmol/L = DKA). Serum: VBG (pH, bicarbonate, pCO₂), electrolytes (corrected sodium, potassium — K⁺ normal or high initially despite total body depletion — critical to monitor when insulin started). Osmolality (calculated). HbA1c (baseline glycaemic control). C-peptide + GAD antibodies (confirm T1DM).
pearls.meds_general: DKA management: (1) Fluid resuscitation: 10 mL/kg 0.9% NaCl bolus if shocked (avoid excessive fluids — cerebral oedema risk). Rehydrate over 48 hours (deficit + maintenance). (2) Insulin: 0.05–0.1 units/kg/hour IV infusion (do NOT start until K⁺ >3.5 mmol/L). (3) Potassium: add 40 mmol/L to fluids when K⁺ <5.5. (4) Dextrose: add 5–10% dextrose when BGL <14 mmol/L (keep glucose 10–14 while acidosis resolves). Cerebral oedema: mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg IV IMMEDIATELY if suspected (deteriorating conscious level, bradycardia, hypertension).

laboratory: U&E (corrected Na, K — monitor 1–2 hourly in DKA)
FBC (leucocytosis common in DKA even without infection)
GAD antibodies, C-peptide, islet cell antibodies (T1DM confirmation)
TFTs (autoimmune thyroid disease — screen at diagnosis)
investigations.key_findings: pH <7.3 + bicarbonate <15 + ketonaemia + hyperglycaemia = DKA. Corrected Na = measured Na + 1.6 × [(glucose − 5.6)/5.6]. If corrected Na falling during treatment = cerebral oedema risk. Potassium critical — falls rapidly when insulin started (K⁺ enters cells).

differentials.name: Hyperglycaemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS)
differentials.distinguishing: Marked hyperglycaemia (>33 mmol/L), minimal ketonuria, hyperosmolality, no acidosis — rare in children, more in T2DM/obese

differentials.name: Gastroenteritis
differentials.distinguishing: Normal glucose; negative ketones on dipstick in proportion; no Kussmaul breathing

differentials.name: Surgical Abdomen (appendicitis)
differentials.distinguishing: DKA can cause abdominal pain — pain should resolve as acidosis corrects; if persists = surgical cause

differentials.name: Meningitis/Encephalitis
differentials.distinguishing: Meningism; normal glucose; CSF abnormal; DKA glucose very high

topic:hypothyroidism_child.name: Hypothyroidism — Childhood (Congenital & Acquired)
topic:hypothyroidism_child.overview: Congenital hypothyroidism (CH): most common preventable cause of intellectual disability worldwide. Incidence 1:3000–4000 live births. Causes: thyroid dysgenesis (75%), dyshormonogenesis (20%). Acquired (Hashimoto's thyroiditis): most common cause of acquired hypothyroidism in children. Iodine deficiency: important in northern Nigeria.

pearls.hpc_onset: Congenital hypothyroidism: classic features appear weeks after birth (protected by maternal thyroid hormones in utero). Newborn screening (TSH heel prick) — not routinely done in most Nigerian hospitals. Late-presenting CH: intellectual disability, short stature, delayed puberty.
pearls.hpc_character: Classic features of CH: prolonged neonatal jaundice, poor feeding, constipation, lethargy ('good baby'), large tongue (macroglossia), hoarse cry, umbilical hernia, large anterior fontanelle, hypothermia. Acquired (Hashimoto's): goitre + gradual onset of hypothyroid symptoms — weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, school performance decline, delayed puberty.
pearls.exam_general: Growth: short stature with delayed bone age. Dry, coarse skin. Puffy face (myxoedema). Bradycardia. Delayed deep tendon reflexes (slow relaxation phase). Macroglossia. Umbilical hernia. Goitre in Hashimoto's (firm, rubbery, non-tender — 'pebbly' texture).
pearls.ix_fbc: TSH (most sensitive test): elevated in primary hypothyroidism. Free T4: low (primary) or low/normal (central hypothyroidism). Anti-TPO antibodies + Anti-Tg antibodies: positive in Hashimoto's. Bone age (X-ray wrist): delayed. Thyroid USS: agenesis/hypoplasia (CH) or heterogeneous parenchyma/enlarged (Hashimoto's).
pearls.meds_general: Levothyroxine (T4): start immediately when diagnosis confirmed — do not wait for aetiology. Dose: neonates/infants 10–15 mcg/kg/day. Children 4–5 mcg/kg/day. Monitor TSH every 4–6 weeks until stable, then 6-monthly. Target TSH: 0.5–2.0 mU/L (lower end in first 3 years for brain development). Compliance is critical — even brief hypothyroidism affects brain development in the first 2–3 years.

differentials.name: Iodine Deficiency (endemic goitre)
differentials.distinguishing: Endemic area (northern Nigeria); soft goitre; TSH mildly elevated; low iodine excretion; treat with iodised salt

differentials.name: Down Syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Characteristic facies; chromosome 21 trisomy; hypothyroidism can co-exist — always check TFTs in Down's

differentials.name: Growth Hormone Deficiency
differentials.distinguishing: Short stature; normal TSH; delayed bone age; GH stimulation test; MRI pituitary

differentials.name: Coeliac Disease
differentials.distinguishing: Failure to thrive; diarrhoea; anti-tTG antibodies; can coexist with Hashimoto's

topic:precocious_puberty.name: Precocious Puberty
topic:precocious_puberty.overview: Pubertal development before age 8 years in girls or age 9 years in boys. Central precocious puberty (CPP): GnRH-dependent (most common in girls — often idiopathic; in boys — usually pathological CNS cause). Peripheral precocious puberty (PPP): GnRH-independent (McCune-Albright, adrenal tumour, gonadal tumour, exogenous oestrogen).

pearls.hpc_onset: In girls: breast development (thelarche) is first sign of puberty. Sequence: thelarche → adrenarche → peak height velocity → menarche. Precocious puberty in a girl aged 6: full work-up needed. In boys: testicular enlargement (>4mL volume, >2.5cm length) is first sign. Any pubertal sign in a boy <9 = investigate.
pearls.hpc_character: CPP: pubertal development proceeds in normal sequence but at inappropriate age. Bone age advances faster than chronological age → early fusion of growth plates → short adult stature if untreated. Associated behaviour changes (emotional lability). PPP: discordant signs — pubic hair/body odour (adrenarche) without breast development, or breast development without pubic hair.
pearls.exam_general: Tanner staging (breast, pubic hair, genital development). Height and weight (advanced growth velocity). Blood pressure (adrenal tumour → hypertension). Café-au-lait spots (McCune-Albright — large, coast-of-Maine border; NF1 — multiple small, smooth border). Abdominal/pelvic exam (adrenal/gonadal mass).
pearls.ix_fbc: Bone age (left wrist X-ray): advanced bone age >2 SD = significant. Baseline LH/FSH (morning sample). GnRH stimulation test: LH peak >5 IU/L = CPP (pubertal response). Oestradiol/testosterone. Adrenal profile (DHEAS, 17-OHP — congenital adrenal hyperplasia). Pelvic USS (ovarian volume, follicles, uterine size — for girls). MRI brain/hypothalamus (to exclude CNS tumour, hamartoma — mandatory in all boys with CPP and girls <6 years).
pearls.meds_general: CPP treatment: GnRH analogue (leuprorelin acetate or triptorelin) IM depot — suppresses HPG axis, arrests pubertal development, allows catch-up growth and bone age maturation. Continue until appropriate pubertal age (~10–11 years in girls). Counselling child and parents regarding puberty, body image, and peer relationships.

differentials.name: Premature Thelarche
differentials.distinguishing: Isolated breast development, no other pubertal signs, <3 years, bone age normal, self-limiting

differentials.name: Premature Adrenarche
differentials.distinguishing: Pubic/axillary hair only, no breast/genital development, DHEAS mildly elevated, bone age normal

differentials.name: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH)
differentials.distinguishing: Ambiguous genitalia at birth (girls); salt-wasting crisis; 17-OHP markedly elevated

differentials.name: McCune-Albright Syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Café-au-lait spots (coast-of-Maine borders); fibrous dysplasia on X-ray; PPP (GnRH-independent)

topic:congenital_adrenal_hyperplasia.name: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH)
topic:congenital_adrenal_hyperplasia.overview: Group of autosomal recessive disorders of adrenal steroidogenesis. 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for 90–95%. Results in cortisol deficiency, aldosterone deficiency (salt-wasting form), and androgen excess. Classic presentation: ambiguous genitalia in newborn girls, salt-wasting crisis in neonatal period, virilisation.

pearls.hpc_onset: Salt-wasting crisis (most common life-threatening presentation): vomiting, poor feeding, lethargy, weight loss, dehydration, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia in the first 2–3 weeks of life. May be confused with pyloric stenosis (no hyperkalaemia in PS) or sepsis.
pearls.hpc_character: Newborn girls: ambiguous genitalia — clitoromegaly, labial fusion, urogenital sinus. Internal female structures normal. Boys: normal genitalia at birth (missed unless screened). Virilising (non-salt-wasting): tall stature + advanced bone age + early pubic hair + small testes (distinguishes from precocious puberty where testes enlarge).
pearls.ix_fbc: 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP): markedly elevated (>100 nmol/L) in 21-OH deficiency. Best taken on day 3–5 of life (normal elevation in first 48h). Electrolytes: hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia = salt-wasting. Cortisol (low). Plasma renin activity (elevated in salt-wasting). ACTH (elevated). Karyotype (all babies with ambiguous genitalia). Pelvic USS (internal anatomy).
pearls.meds_general: Acute salt-wasting crisis: IV 0.9% NaCl + 10% dextrose (correct hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia). IV hydrocortisone (stress dose: 25 mg/m² then 50–100 mg/m²/day). Fludrocortisone for mineralocorticoid replacement. Chronic: hydrocortisone 10–15 mg/m²/day in 3 divided doses (glucocorticoid replacement). Fludrocortisone 0.05–0.2 mg/day (mineralocorticoid). Salt supplementation in infancy. Monitor growth, bone age, 17-OHP, plasma renin — balance between under- and over-treatment.

virilisation: Tall child → short adult (early epiphyseal fusion)

differentials.name: Pyloric Stenosis
differentials.distinguishing: Vomiting but hypokalaemia (not hyperkalaemia); normal 17-OHP; olive mass; ultrasound

differentials.name: Neonatal Sepsis
differentials.distinguishing: Blood culture positive; 17-OHP normal; no electrolyte pattern

differentials.name: Disorders of Sexual Development (DSD)
differentials.distinguishing: Karyotype, hormonal, USS, and specialist assessment required — CAH is one cause of DSD

differentials.name: Addison's Disease
differentials.distinguishing: Primary adrenal insufficiency without androgen excess; normal 17-OHP; autoimmune

topic:anaemia_child.name: Anaemia in Childhood — Approach and Iron Deficiency Anaemia
topic:anaemia_child.overview: Anaemia (Hb below age-specific threshold) is extremely common in Nigerian children. WHO defines anaemia: <6 months: Hb <13.5 g/dL; 6 months–5 years: Hb <11 g/dL; 5–11 years: Hb <11.5 g/dL; adolescents: Hb <12 g/dL (girls), <13 g/dL (boys). Iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) is the most common cause globally. In Nigeria: malaria, IDA, haemoglobinopathies, and nutritional deficiencies overlap.

pearls.hpc_onset: Determine rate of onset — acute (haemolysis, haemorrhage → compensatory mechanisms overwhelmed, severe symptoms) vs chronic (IDA, haemoglobinopathy → gradual adaptation, symptoms appear at lower Hb). A child with Hb 5 g/dL from chronic IDA may look well; a child with Hb 8 g/dL from acute haemolysis may be in shock.
pearls.hpc_character: IDA symptoms: pallor, fatigue, poor school performance, irritability, pica (craving non-food items — soil/chalk = pagophagia), poor feeding in infants. Haemolytic anaemia: jaundice + pallor + dark urine. Aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19 in SCD): sudden severe pallor without jaundice.
pearls.exam_general: Pallor assessment: conjunctival pallor (most reliable), palmar pallor, nail bed pallor. Jaundice (haemolysis). Splenomegaly (haemolytic anaemia, malaria, thalassaemia). Lymphadenopathy + hepatosplenomegaly (leukaemia, lymphoma). Cardiac: flow murmur, hyperdynamic apex, gallop (severe anaemia → cardiac failure). Frontal bossing, tower skull (thalassaemia, SCD — extramedullary haematopoiesis).
pearls.ix_fbc: FBC: Hb, MCV, MCH, MCHC, reticulocyte count. MCV interpretation: Microcytic (MCV <80): IDA (ferritin low, TIBC high), thalassaemia (ferritin normal), chronic disease. Normocytic (MCV 80–100): haemolysis (reticulocytes elevated), chronic disease, aplastic anaemia, acute blood loss. Macrocytic (MCV >100): folate/B12 deficiency. Peripheral blood film (key): hypochromic microcytic (IDA), target cells (thalassaemia/SCD), sickle cells, malarial parasites, hypersegmented neutrophils (B12/folate).
pearls.ix_lft: Iron studies: serum ferritin <12 ng/mL (IDA — most specific), low serum iron, elevated TIBC. Reticulocyte count: elevated (haemolysis, haemorrhage, treatment response); low (aplastic, IDA). Haemoglobin electrophoresis (SCD, thalassaemia). Coombs test (immune haemolytic anaemia). G6PD assay. Malaria film/RDT (co-existent malaria).
pearls.meds_general: IDA: oral ferrous sulphate 3–6 mg/kg/day elemental iron for minimum 3 months (1 month to correct Hb + 2 months to replenish stores). Give on empty stomach (absorption), with Vitamin C (enhances absorption), away from milk/tea (inhibits). Monitor Hb at 4 weeks (should rise 1–2 g/dL). Continue for 3 months total after Hb normalises. Address dietary causes and treat underlying infection (malaria, hookworm).

differentials.name: Thalassaemia
differentials.distinguishing: Microcytic anaemia + normal/elevated ferritin + target cells on film + Hb electrophoresis abnormal + Mediterranean/Asian origin

differentials.name: Malaria-associated Anaemia
differentials.distinguishing: Positive blood film/RDT; haemolysis + dyserythropoiesis; responds to antimalarials

differentials.name: Leukaemia
differentials.distinguishing: Pancytopaenia; blast cells on film; lymphadenopathy; hepatosplenomegaly; bone marrow biopsy

differentials.name: Aplastic Anaemia
differentials.distinguishing: Pancytopaenia; low reticulocytes; hypocellular bone marrow; no splenomegaly

topic:idiopathic_thrombocytopaenic_purpu.name: Immune Thrombocytopaenic Purpura (ITP)
topic:idiopathic_thrombocytopaenic_purpu.overview: Immune-mediated destruction of platelets by anti-platelet IgG antibodies. Childhood ITP: usually acute, self-limiting, often post-viral (1–6 weeks after URTI or viral illness). Peak age: 2–8 years. Most children recover within 6 months. 20–30% develop chronic ITP (>12 months). Distinguished from other causes of purpura by: isolated thrombocytopaenia + well-looking child.

pearls.hpc_onset: Acute onset of purpura/bruising in a well-looking, previously healthy child — often 2–4 weeks after viral illness (EBV, CMV, URTI, varicella, measles vaccine). The child looks WELL despite dramatic rash — this is a key distinguishing feature from meningococcal purpura (child looks very unwell, shocked).
pearls.hpc_character: Bruising in unusual sites (trunk, face, ears), petechiae, mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia in adolescent girls), wet purpura (haemorrhagic blisters in mouth — risk of intracranial haemorrhage). Intracranial haemorrhage: <1% risk, occurs when platelets <10 × 10⁹/L with head trauma or very low counts.
pearls.exam_skin: Petechiae (non-blanching — pinpoint red/purple spots on skin), purpura (non-blanching, >3mm), ecchymoses (bruises in unusual sites). Rash is flat (non-palpable) — distinguishes from HSP (palpable/raised purpura). Child is well — no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly (if present → consider leukaemia).
pearls.ix_fbc: FBC: isolated thrombocytopaenia (platelets <100 × 10⁹/L; often <20 × 10⁹/L). Normal Hb and WBC — pancytopaenia would suggest leukaemia/aplastic anaemia. Blood film: normal RBCs and WBCs, reduced platelets, megathrombocytes (large platelets — active production). Bone marrow: NOT routinely needed unless atypical features. Coagulation screen: normal PT and APTT (distinguishes from DIC).
pearls.meds_general: Observation alone: well child with dry purpura (no mucosal bleeding) regardless of platelet count. Treatment (wet purpura, significant bleeding, or platelets <10 × 10⁹/L): IV anti-D (if Rh positive) or IVIG 0.8–1 g/kg (raises platelets in 24–48h). Oral prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg × 14 days then taper. Platelet transfusion only for life-threatening haemorrhage (short-lived due to rapid destruction). Avoid NSAIDs, aspirin, IM injections, contact sports.

symptoms: NO systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, arthritis — if present, reconsider diagnosis)
signs: Wet purpura / mucosal haematoma (severe — high ICH risk)
Child LOOKS WELL — no fever, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly

differentials.name: Meningococcal Septicaemia
differentials.distinguishing: Child looks VERY ILL; petechiae spreading rapidly; shock; fever; blood culture positive — EMERGENCY

differentials.name: HSP (IgA Vasculitis)
differentials.distinguishing: Palpable purpura (raised); lower limbs/buttocks; arthritis; abdominal pain; normal platelets

differentials.name: Leukaemia
differentials.distinguishing: Pancytopaenia; blast cells on film; lymphadenopathy; bone pain; hepatosplenomegaly

differentials.name: DIC
differentials.distinguishing: Prolonged PT/APTT; low fibrinogen; elevated D-dimers; underlying sepsis/malignancy

differentials.name: Non-accidental Injury (NAI)
differentials.distinguishing: Bruises of different ages; unusual pattern; inconsistent history; safeguarding concerns

topic:thalassaemia.name: Thalassaemia
topic:thalassaemia.overview: Inherited disorders of haemoglobin chain synthesis. Beta-thalassaemia major (Cooley's anaemia): severe transfusion-dependent anaemia from infancy. Less common in Nigeria compared to West/North Africa, but important to recognise. Alpha-thalassaemia more common in Nigeria. Haemoglobin H disease and haemoglobin Barts (hydrops fetalis) are alpha-thalassaemia major presentations.

pearls.hpc_onset: Beta-thalassaemia major presents at 6–12 months of age when HbF declines and HbA production fails. Presents with severe anaemia (Hb 3–6 g/dL), failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, bony changes. Nigeria: co-inheritance with HbS produces HbS-Beta thalassaemia — similar to SCD.
pearls.exam_general: Classic features: frontal bossing, tower skull, prominent cheekbones, maxillary overgrowth (dental malocclusion), 'chipmunk facies' — all from marrow expansion due to ineffective erythropoiesis. Massive hepatosplenomegaly. Pallor. Jaundice (haemolysis). Short stature. Delayed puberty (iron overload affecting pituitary).
pearls.ix_fbc: FBC: severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia (Hb 3–7 g/dL), normal/elevated ferritin (OPPOSITE of IDA), elevated reticulocytes (but less than expected for degree of anaemia — ineffective erythropoiesis). Blood film: target cells, nucleated RBCs, hypochromic microcytes, basophilic stippling, Pappenheimer bodies. HbEPG (electrophoresis): absent/reduced HbA, elevated HbA2 (>3.5%), elevated HbF. Serum ferritin (iron overload monitoring). LFTs (liver iron overload). TFTs, ECHO (endocrine and cardiac complications of iron overload).
pearls.meds_general: Regular blood transfusions every 3–4 weeks (maintain pre-transfusion Hb >9–10 g/dL). Iron chelation: essential to prevent iron overload (transfusion haemosiderosis). Deferasirox (oral, first-line) or desferrioxamine (subcutaneous overnight infusion). Curative: bone marrow transplant (if HLA-matched sibling available). Folic acid supplementation. Splenectomy (if hypersplenism — rising transfusion requirements). Genetic counselling.

differentials.name: Iron Deficiency Anaemia
differentials.distinguishing: Low ferritin; normal Hb electrophoresis; no bony changes; responds to iron

differentials.name: Sickle Cell Disease
differentials.distinguishing: HbEPG shows HbSS; pain crises; autosplenectomy; Nigerian descent common

differentials.name: Leukaemia
differentials.distinguishing: Pancytopaenia; blast cells; lymphadenopathy; rapid progression

topic:acute_leukaemia_child.name: Acute Leukaemia — Childhood
topic:acute_leukaemia_child.overview: Most common childhood malignancy. ALL (Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia): 75–80% — peak age 2–5 years. AML (Acute Myeloid Leukaemia): 15–20%. ALL in childhood has >90% cure rate in high-income countries; outcomes poor in Nigeria due to treatment abandonment, infections, and access issues. Burkitt's lymphoma (B-ALL variant) is common in sub-Saharan Africa (EBV-associated, jaw mass).

pearls.hpc_onset: Insidious onset of constitutional symptoms over weeks: fatigue, pallor, recurrent infections, bruising, bone pain (children hold limb rigid, refuse to walk — metaphyseal pain from marrow infiltration). Night sweats and weight loss. Burkitt's lymphoma: rapidly enlarging jaw/abdominal mass (days to weeks).
pearls.hpc_character: Pancytopaenia triad: (1) Anaemia → pallor, fatigue. (2) Neutropaenia → recurrent infections (fever without focus). (3) Thrombocytopaenia → bruising, petechiae. Bone pain + pancytopaenia = leukaemia until proven otherwise. Mediastinal mass (T-ALL) → superior vena cava syndrome (facial swelling, dyspnoea, stridor).
pearls.exam_general: Lymphadenopathy (generalised — cervical, axillary, inguinal). Hepatosplenomegaly (leukaemic infiltration). Testicular enlargement (ALL — sanctuary site). Fundoscopy (retinal haemorrhage, leukaemic infiltrates). Skin: petechiae, ecchymoses. Gum hypertrophy (AML-M5, monocytic leukaemia).
pearls.ix_fbc: FBC: pancytopaenia (all three cell lines low). Leucocytosis with blasts on film: WBC may be very high (hyperleucocytosis >100 × 10⁹/L = leukaemia crisis — risk of tumour lysis syndrome). Blast cells on peripheral blood film (may be absent — aleukemic leukaemia). Bone marrow biopsy + aspirate: >20–25% blasts = acute leukaemia. Immunophenotyping (flow cytometry) — B-ALL, T-ALL, AML. Cytogenetics (translocation t(12;21) in ALL = favourable; t(9;22)/BCR-ABL = poor prognosis). LDH (elevated = high tumour burden). Uric acid (tumour lysis). CXR (mediastinal mass — T-ALL). LP (CSF) — CNS disease.
pearls.meds_general: ALL treatment: induction (vincristine + prednisolone + asparaginase + intrathecal methotrexate) → consolidation → maintenance (oral mercaptopurine + methotrexate × 2 years). CNS prophylaxis: intrathecal chemotherapy (replaces cranial radiotherapy). Tumour lysis syndrome prophylaxis: IV fluids + allopurinol + monitor electrolytes/uric acid/creatinine. Burkitt's (BL-ALL): CODOX-M/IVAC or BFM-based regimen — intense but shorter (3–6 months, rapidly proliferating tumour). Treatment abandonment is the biggest challenge in Nigeria — counselling, social support essential.

differentials.name: ITP
differentials.distinguishing: Isolated thrombocytopaenia; no lymphadenopathy; well child; normal Hb and WBC

differentials.name: Aplastic Anaemia
differentials.distinguishing: Pancytopaenia; no blasts; hypocellular bone marrow; no lymphadenopathy

differentials.name: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Joint swelling; morning stiffness; ANA; no pancytopaenia; no blasts

differentials.name: Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV)
differentials.distinguishing: Reactive lymphocytes (not blasts); positive Monospot/EBV serology; tonsillopharyngitis; rash with amoxicillin

topic:wilms_tumour.name: Wilms' Tumour (Nephroblastoma)
topic:wilms_tumour.overview: Most common primary renal tumour of childhood. Peak age: 3–4 years. Accounts for 90% of paediatric renal tumours. Associated with aniridia, hemihypertrophy, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, WAGR syndrome. Cure rate >85% with treatment (surgery + chemotherapy + radiotherapy in selected cases).

pearls.hpc_onset: Classic presentation: painless abdominal mass discovered incidentally by parent or during bath. Typically unilateral. Child often looks well despite massive tumour. Haematuria (25%), hypertension (25% — renin-secreting tumour), abdominal pain.
pearls.exam_abdomen: Large, smooth, non-tender flank mass that does NOT cross the midline (distinguishes from neuroblastoma which does cross midline). Mass moves with respiration. Beware of rupturing during examination — handle VERY GENTLY (tumour rupture → peritoneal seeding). DO NOT perform multiple repeated palpations.
pearls.ix_fbc: Abdominal USS (first-line): solid renal mass, distortion of normal renal architecture, IVC extension (10% — assess for tumour thrombus). CT abdomen/chest (staging): extent of tumour, lymph nodes, liver metastases, pulmonary metastases. CXR (lung mets). Urinalysis (haematuria). FBC, U&E, LFTs. Biopsy: only if diagnosis uncertain or bilateral (SIOP protocol — preoperative chemotherapy then surgery).
pearls.meds_general: COG protocol: immediate nephrectomy + chemotherapy (vincristine + actinomycin-D ± doxorubicin ± radiotherapy depending on stage and histology). SIOP protocol (used in Europe and many African centres): preoperative chemotherapy × 4 weeks → nephrectomy → adjuvant chemotherapy. 5-year survival: stage I (>95%), stage IV (pulmonary mets, ~85%). Bilateral Wilms' (5%): more complex — bilateral nephron-sparing surgery + chemotherapy.

signs: Associated anomalies: aniridia, hemihypertrophy, genitourinary anomalies

differentials.name: Neuroblastoma
differentials.distinguishing: Crosses the midline; harder, irregular mass; catecholamine excess; younger age <2; VMA/HVA elevated

differentials.name: Hydronephrosis
differentials.distinguishing: Smooth, transilluminates (in neonates); USS shows dilated renal pelvis; not solid

differentials.name: Multicystic Dysplastic Kidney
differentials.distinguishing: Non-functioning kidney; cystic on USS; no solid component

differentials.name: Renal Cell Carcinoma
differentials.distinguishing: Rare in children; older age group; different histology

topic:cerebral_malaria_vs_meningitis.name: Cerebral Malaria vs Bacterial Meningitis — Differential Approach
topic:cerebral_malaria_vs_meningitis.overview: One of the most critical and common diagnostic challenges in Nigerian paediatric practice. Both present with fever + seizures + altered consciousness. Co-infection is possible (5–10% of cases). Key principle: in endemic areas, TREAT BOTH while awaiting results — do not wait for confirmation before starting treatment.

pearls.hpc_onset: Rapid-onset coma (hours): favours cerebral malaria. Coma following progressive headache + meningism over 12–24h: favours meningitis. Purpuric rash + shock = meningococcal septicaemia — treat immediately. Neither pattern is exclusive — co-infection occurs.
pearls.exam_neuro: Meningism (neck stiffness, Kernig's, Brudzinski's): present in meningitis, ABSENT or minimal in cerebral malaria. Retinal haemorrhages (fundoscopy): pathognomonic of cerebral malaria — not seen in bacterial meningitis. BCS/GCS: both cause impaired consciousness, but cerebral malaria may have decorticate/decerebrate posturing.
pearls.ix_fbc: Immediate investigations: (1) Malaria RDT/film — positive = cerebral malaria (but does NOT exclude co-infection). (2) Blood culture. (3) Blood glucose (both cause hypoglycaemia). LP (if no contraindication): CSF turbid + neutrophilia + low glucose = bacterial meningitis. Clear CSF = viral or cerebral malaria. Note: in cerebral malaria, CSF may have mild pleocytosis (up to 20 cells) — do not over-interpret.
pearls.meds_general: In-practice approach when unsure: Start BOTH IV artesunate (severe malaria) AND IV ceftriaxone (bacterial meningitis) simultaneously while awaiting results. This is the safest approach in a resource-limited setting. Dexamethasone: beneficial in bacterial meningitis (Hib/pneumococcal) — NOT beneficial in cerebral malaria (harmful in some studies — use only after excluding malaria or use cautiously).

cerebral_malaria: Blantyre Coma Scale correlates with outcome
bacterial_meningitis: CSF: turbid, neutrophilia, low glucose, high protein

topic:failure_to_thrive.name: Failure to Thrive (Faltering Growth)
topic:failure_to_thrive.overview: Inadequate physical growth: weight for age crossing ≥2 centile lines downward, or weight persistently below 3rd centile. Classified as: organic (underlying disease), non-organic (environmental/psychosocial — inadequate intake), or mixed (most common). In Nigeria: commonest causes are inadequate dietary intake, recurrent infections (especially malaria, diarrhoea), and SAM.

pearls.hpc_onset: Growth chart analysis is the foundation: plot weight, height, and head circumference on appropriate growth chart. Key patterns: (1) Weight crosses centiles first, then height, then head circumference (HC) = nutritional/environmental (non-organic first). (2) Weight and height fall together = constitutional short stature, skeletal dysplasia. (3) HC falls with weight/height = CNS pathology or IUGR. (4) Height crosses centiles only = endocrine (hypothyroidism, GHD).
pearls.hpc_character: Nutritional history: 24-hour diet recall, feeding history (breast vs bottle, weaning practices), meal frequency, family food security. Infection history: recurrent diarrhoea, malaria, RTIs. Psychosocial: carer-child interaction, maternal depression, poverty, domestic violence, food insecurity.
pearls.exam_general: Anthropometry: weight-for-age, height-for-age, weight-for-height, MUAC, head circumference. SAM: MUAC <11.5cm, WHZ <-3, bilateral oedema. Organic causes: dysmorphic features (chromosomal), congenital heart defect, abdominal signs (coeliac, IBD), neurological (swallowing difficulty, hypotonia).
pearls.ix_fbc: Investigations should be targeted by history/exam — not blanket investigations. Minimum screen: FBC + film (anaemia, parasites), U&E, LFTs, TFTs (hypothyroidism), urine MC&S (UTI), stool (parasites — Giardia, Strongyloides), malaria RDT. Coeliac: anti-tTG IgA (if dietary gluten exposure). HIV test (all children with FTT in Nigeria). Consider: sweat test (CF), chromosomes, echocardiogram.
pearls.meds_general: Non-organic FTT: nutritional rehabilitation, high-calorie supplementation, treat infections, social support, carer education. MDT approach: paediatrician, dietitian, social worker, health visitor. Organic FTT: treat underlying cause. Safeguarding assessment: if neglect/abuse suspected. Growth monitoring: monthly until normal centile maintained.

differentials.name: Constitutional Short Stature
differentials.distinguishing: Short but normal growth velocity; family history of short stature; bone age normal; will reach normal adult height

differentials.name: Familial Short Stature
differentials.distinguishing: Short parents; normal growth velocity; bone age = chronological age; predicted adult height appropriate

differentials.name: Growth Hormone Deficiency
differentials.distinguishing: Height falls more than weight; delayed bone age; GH stimulation test abnormal; MRI pituitary

differentials.name: Coeliac Disease
differentials.distinguishing: Diarrhoea + bloating; anti-tTG antibodies; villous atrophy on biopsy; responds to gluten-free diet

differentials.name: Chronic Malnutrition (stunting)
differentials.distinguishing: Height-for-age Z-score <-2; chronic process; weight-for-height may be normal (stunted, not wasted)

topic:juvenile_idiopathic_arthritis.name: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA)
topic:juvenile_idiopathic_arthritis.overview: Heterogeneous group of chronic inflammatory arthritides beginning before age 16, lasting >6 weeks, with no identified cause. Classified into 7 subtypes (ILAR criteria): systemic JIA (Still's disease), oligoarticular (most common in Europe, less in Nigeria), polyarticular RF-positive, polyarticular RF-negative, enthesitis-related arthritis, psoriatic, undifferentiated.

pearls.hpc_onset: Joint stiffness is worse in the MORNING (morning stiffness) — characteristic of inflammatory arthritis. Improves with activity (opposite to degenerative). Child prefers NOT to move the joint. Limp or joint protection posture. Duration >6 weeks required for diagnosis.
pearls.hpc_character: Systemic JIA (Still's disease): daily quotidian salmon-pink rash (evanescent — appears with fever spike then disappears), high spiking fever (>39°C once or twice daily), hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, serositis (pericarditis, pleuritis). Most severe subtype — macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) is a life-threatening complication.
pearls.exam_general: Joint examination: warmth, swelling, tenderness, range of motion, effusion. Systemic JIA rash: salmon-pink, macular, evanescent (appears during fever spike). Uveitis (anterior): insidious, often asymptomatic — detected on slit-lamp examination. Key complication: blindness from chronic uveitis (oligoarticular ANA-positive JIA). Monitor for Cushingoid features (steroid use).
pearls.ix_fbc: Systemic JIA: very high WBC (neutrophilia), very high ferritin (>10,000 in MAS — markedly elevated, >5 times upper limit = MAS), elevated ESR/CRP, anaemia. RF (IgM rheumatoid factor): positive only in RF-positive polyarticular subtype. ANA: positive in oligoarticular (risk of uveitis). Anti-CCP (early erosive disease). Slit-lamp exam: ALL JIA patients require regular ophthalmology screening for uveitis.
pearls.meds_general: NSAIDs (naproxen, ibuprofen): first-line for all subtypes. Corticosteroids: intra-articular injection (oligoarticular), systemic (systemic JIA, MAS). Methotrexate: second-line disease-modifying agent (weekly dose with folic acid). Biologics (second/third-line — expensive, limited availability in Nigeria): TNF inhibitors (etanercept, adalimumab) for polyarticular; IL-1 inhibitors (anakinra, canakinumab) for systemic JIA. MAS (systemic JIA complication): high-dose IV methylprednisolone + ciclosporin.

differentials.name: Septic Arthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Monoarticular; toxic appearance; very hot, swollen; WBC very high; joint aspiration purulent; blood culture

differentials.name: Acute Rheumatic Fever
differentials.distinguishing: Migratory polyarthritis; ASO elevated; carditis; chorea; responds dramatically to aspirin

differentials.name: Reactive Arthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Preceded by GI/GU infection; asymmetric oligoarthritis; HLA-B27 positive; self-limiting

differentials.name: Leukaemia
differentials.distinguishing: Bone pain; pancytopaenia; blast cells; hepatosplenomegaly; ferritin very high — distinguish from systemic JIA

differentials.name: SLE
differentials.distinguishing: Adolescent female; photosensitive rash; multi-system; ANA/dsDNA positive; low complement

topic:otitis_media_child.name: Acute Otitis Media (AOM)
topic:otitis_media_child.overview: Most common bacterial infection in children worldwide. Peak age: 6 months to 2 years. Risk factors: daycare attendance, passive smoke exposure, formula feeding, craniofacial anomalies (Down syndrome, cleft palate), bottle feeding lying flat. Common organisms: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis.

pearls.hpc_onset: Ear pain (otalgia) is the cardinal symptom — infants may pull at ears, be irritable, cry inconsolably especially at night (recumbent position increases middle ear pressure). Often follows 2–3 days of URTI (viral URTI → Eustachian tube dysfunction → secondary bacterial infection). Fever.
pearls.hpc_character: AOM vs OME (otitis media with effusion): AOM = acute pain + fever + bulging TM + effusion. OME (glue ear) = chronic effusion without inflammation (no pain, no fever) — main concern is conductive hearing loss affecting speech development. Perforated AOM: sudden relief of pain → purulent discharge from ear — often means TM has perforated.
pearls.exam_general: Otoscopy (essential): TM appearance — normal (grey, translucent, light reflex visible), AOM (red, bulging, opacified, no light reflex, effusion behind TM). Perforation: hole in TM + purulent discharge. Pneumatic otoscopy: absent/reduced TM mobility = effusion. Mastoid tenderness: mastoiditis complication.
pearls.ix_fbc: Clinical diagnosis — no investigations usually needed. Consider: tympanometry (effusion), audiogram (hearing loss — OME), CT mastoid (if mastoiditis suspected — postauricular swelling, ear displaced forward). Blood culture if systemically unwell.
pearls.meds_general: Watchful waiting (observation): AOM in children >2 years with mild-moderate symptoms (no fever >39°C, well-looking) — most resolve in 72 hours. Prescribe antibiotics to fill but advise parent to start only if no improvement in 48–72 hours (delayed prescription). Antibiotics if: <6 months, bilateral AOM, otalgia >48h, high fever, not improving in 48–72h. First-line: amoxicillin 40–90 mg/kg/day × 5–7 days. Penicillin allergic: azithromycin. Analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen) essential — addresses pain. Grommets (tympanostomy tubes): recurrent AOM (≥3 in 6 months or ≥4 in 12 months) or persistent OME with hearing loss.

symptoms: Ear pain (otalgia) / ear pulling in infants
signs: Opacified TM with fluid level or air bubbles

differentials.name: External Otitis (Swimmer's Ear)
differentials.distinguishing: Pain on tragal compression or pinna movement; moist, inflamed EAC; no TM bulging; water exposure

differentials.name: Otitis Media with Effusion (OME)
differentials.distinguishing: No pain/fever; TM retracted or amber-coloured; hearing loss; tympanometry type B

differentials.name: Mastoiditis
differentials.distinguishing: Postauricular swelling + tenderness; ear displaced forward/downward; CT confirms

differentials.name: Teething (infants)
differentials.distinguishing: Drooling; irritability; no TM changes on otoscopy; normal otoscopy

topic:tonsillitis_child.name: Tonsillitis & Pharyngitis
topic:tonsillitis_child.overview: Inflammation of the tonsils (tonsillitis) and pharynx (pharyngitis). Commonest cause of sore throat in children. Viral (70–80%): adenovirus, EBV, enteroviruses. Bacterial (20–30%): Group A Streptococcus (GAS/Strep pyogenes) — important to identify (risk of acute rheumatic fever in Nigeria).

pearls.hpc_onset: GAS pharyngitis features: sudden onset sore throat, high fever, tonsillar exudate, anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, NO cough, NO coryza. Viral pharyngitis: gradual onset, URTI symptoms (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), lower fever. Centor score (modified McIsaac): 1 point each for — tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical LN, fever >38°C, absent cough, age <15 years.
pearls.hpc_character: Complications of GAS: peritonsillar abscess (quinsy — unilateral tonsillar swelling, uvular deviation, 'hot potato' voice, trismus, drooling). Retropharyngeal abscess. Acute rheumatic fever (2–4 weeks post-infection). Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (1–3 weeks post-infection). Scarlet fever: GAS + scarlatiniform rash (sandpaper texture, flushed face, circumoral pallor).
pearls.exam_general: Throat: tonsillar erythema, exudate (white/yellow plaques — GAS, EBV), tonsillar enlargement (grading 1–4). Lymphadenopathy: tender anterior cervical LN (GAS), posterior cervical + inguinal + axillary (EBV). Splenomegaly (EBV — avoid contact sports, risk of splenic rupture). Scarlet fever: sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor.
pearls.ix_fbc: Throat swab culture (gold standard): 24–48h for GAS confirmation. Rapid antigen detection test (RADT): GAS antigen — sensitivity 70–90%, specificity >95%. FBC: lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes = EBV. Monospot test (heterophile antibody): positive EBV (sensitivity 85% in children >5 years). EBV-specific serology (VCA IgM/IgG) — more sensitive. ASO titre (post-GAS — elevated within 2 weeks).
pearls.meds_general: Viral tonsillitis: symptomatic (paracetamol/ibuprofen, adequate fluids). No antibiotics. GAS tonsillitis: penicillin V 250mg (children) 4× daily × 10 days (amoxicillin acceptable, but AVOID amoxicillin in EBV — causes morbilliform rash in ~90%). Penicillin allergy: azithromycin or erythromycin. Tonsillectomy: indicated for recurrent tonsillitis (≥7 episodes in 1 year, ≥5 per year × 2 years, ≥3 per year × 3 years — Paradise criteria). Peritonsillar abscess: needle aspiration or incision + drainage + IV antibiotics.

ebv_features: Exudative tonsillitis + posterior cervical/generalised LN + splenomegaly

differentials.name: Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV)
differentials.distinguishing: Generalised lymphadenopathy + splenomegaly; atypical lymphocytes; monospot positive; fatigue

differentials.name: Diphtheria
differentials.distinguishing: Grey pseudomembrane (cannot be scraped off); bull-neck; toxin effects; not vaccinated (DTP)

differentials.name: Peritonsillar Abscess
differentials.distinguishing: Unilateral swelling; uvular deviation; trismus; muffled voice; requires drainage

differentials.name: Retropharyngeal Abscess
differentials.distinguishing: Neck stiffness; drooling; muffled voice; CT soft tissue neck — posterior pharyngeal swelling

topic:developmental_delay.name: Global Developmental Delay & Developmental Assessment
topic:developmental_delay.overview: Developmental delay: failure to achieve developmental milestones in one or more domains (gross motor, fine motor, language/communication, personal-social) at the expected age. Global developmental delay (GDD): significant delay in ≥2 domains in children <5 years. Intellectual disability: diagnosis after age 5 when formal cognitive testing possible.

pearls.hpc_onset: Detailed developmental history is essential. Ask specifically about each domain: (1) Gross motor: head control (4mo), sitting unsupported (6–9mo), pulling to stand (9–12mo), walking unsupported (12–18mo). (2) Fine motor/vision: hand regard (3mo), palmar grasp (4mo), pincer grip (9–10mo). (3) Language/hearing: cooing (2mo), babbling (6mo), first words (12mo), 2-word phrases (18–24mo). (4) Social: social smile (6–8 weeks), stranger anxiety (6–9mo), imitative play (12mo), symbolic play (18mo).
pearls.hpc_character: Regression (loss of previously acquired skills) is always pathological — investigate urgently: metabolic disease, SSPE, Rett syndrome, neurodegeneration. Isolated speech delay vs global delay: isolated speech delay — check hearing first (conductive hearing loss from OME is commonest preventable cause of speech delay).
pearls.pmh_general: Birth history: gestational age, complications, birth weight, Apgar scores, NICU admission. Perinatal: HIE, neonatal sepsis, neonatal jaundice (kernicterus). Family history: consanguinity (metabolic/genetic), siblings with similar issues, parental education level. Social history: primary caregiver, stimulation at home, daycare, nutrition.
pearls.exam_neuro: Neurocutaneous markers: ash-leaf spots (Wood's lamp — tuberous sclerosis), café-au-lait spots (NF1), port-wine stain (Sturge-Weber), adenoma sebaceum. Dysmorphic features (Down syndrome, Fragile X — macro-orchidism + prominent ears). Head circumference: microcephaly (structural brain damage, genetic, TORCH), macrocephaly (hydrocephalus, storage disease, achondroplasia). Tone: hypotonia (Down's, SMA, hypothyroidism, metabolic) vs hypertonia (CP, spastic syndromes).
pearls.ix_fbc: Targeted investigations: Hearing test (all children with speech delay). Vision assessment. TFTs (hypothyroidism — treatable). Chromosomes/karyotype (dysmorphic features). Fragile X DNA test. Metabolic screen (amino acids, organic acids, lactate, ammonia). MRI brain (structural abnormality, white matter disease). EEG (epilepsy). TORCH screen (congenital infection). Bone age (endocrine causes). Lead level (high-risk children — pica, old paint exposure).

gross_motor.2yr: Runs, kicks ball, up stairs 2 feet/step

social.12mo: Symbolic play begins, separation anxiety peak

red_flags: Any skill regression at any age

differentials.name: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
differentials.distinguishing: Social communication deficit + restricted interests + repetitive behaviours; language delay but also social impairment; M-CHAT-R screen

differentials.name: Specific Language Impairment
differentials.distinguishing: Language delay only; normal non-verbal IQ; normal social development; hearing normal

differentials.name: Hearing Impairment
differentials.distinguishing: Speech delay disproportionate to other domains; audiometry; PASS/REFER newborn hearing screen

differentials.name: Intellectual Disability
differentials.distinguishing: Global impairment across all domains; aetiology investigation as above

topic:autism_spectrum_disorder.name: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
topic:autism_spectrum_disorder.overview: Neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by persistent deficits in social communication/interaction AND restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour/interests/activities. Onset in early developmental period (usually apparent by age 2–3 years). Prevalence: ~1 in 100 children globally. Under-recognised in Nigeria due to cultural beliefs and limited diagnostic services.

pearls.hpc_onset: Parents often report: 'He was normal then stopped talking.' Regression: loss of language skills (50 words → none) at 15–24 months is classic. But more commonly: normal early milestones then subtle but persistent social communication differences noted. Red flags: no pointing (declarative) by 12 months, no joint attention, no response to name, absent pretend play.
pearls.hpc_character: Three core domains: (1) Social communication: limited eye contact, failure to point or share interest, does not respond to name, limited facial expression, no pretend play. (2) Restricted/repetitive behaviours: lining up toys, insistence on sameness (routines), stereotypies (hand-flapping, rocking), intense focused interests, hypersensitivity/hyposensitivity to sensory input. (3) Language: may be absent, echoed (echolalia — repeating phrases from TV), or pedantic.
pearls.exam_neuro: M-CHAT-R (Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised) — screening tool for age 16–30 months. ADOS-2 (Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule) — gold standard diagnostic assessment. Neurological exam: usually normal. Look for associated features: intellectual disability (30–50%), epilepsy (25%), ADHD, anxiety, tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf spots — ASD association).
pearls.ix_fbc: Hearing test (MUST do in all speech delayed children — exclude before ASD diagnosis). Chromosomes/microarray (fragile X, deletions, duplications). Metabolic screen (if regression — exclude treatable metabolic cause). EEG (if seizures). MRI brain (focal findings, tuberous sclerosis). Lead level (pica is common in ASD). Thyroid function.
pearls.meds_general: No cure — management is supportive and educational. Early intensive behavioural intervention (ABA — Applied Behaviour Analysis): best evidence, but expensive and resource-limited in Nigeria. Speech and language therapy. Occupational therapy (sensory integration). Special educational needs. Parent/carer training is fundamental. Pharmacological: risperidone or aripiprazole (irritability/aggression in ASD — FDA approved). Melatonin (sleep disturbance). Treat co-existing ADHD, epilepsy, anxiety.

social_communication: Absent joint attention (pointing to share interest)

differentials.name: Global Developmental Delay
differentials.distinguishing: Delay across all domains; social development delayed but not specifically impaired; no restricted interests

differentials.name: Specific Language Impairment
differentials.distinguishing: Language only delayed; normal social interaction and play; normal non-verbal skills

differentials.name: Hearing Impairment
differentials.distinguishing: Speech delay; turns to loud sounds; audiometry abnormal; social skills intact

differentials.name: Social Communication Disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Social communication deficit WITHOUT restricted/repetitive behaviours — on the spectrum boundary

differentials.name: Rett Syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Girls only; normal development then regression at 6–18 months; stereotyped hand-wringing; MECP2 mutation

topic:attention_deficit_hyperactivity.name: ADHD — Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
topic:attention_deficit_hyperactivity.overview: Neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that is pervasive (present in ≥2 settings), developmentally inappropriate, and impairing. Prevalence: 5–10% of school-age children. 3× more common in boys. Subtypes: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, combined (most common). Significant under-recognition in Nigeria.

pearls.hpc_onset: Onset before age 12 (DSM-5). Symptoms present for ≥6 months. Pervasive: must be present in ≥2 settings (home AND school). Impairment: academic, social, or occupational. School-age presentation: academic underachievement despite normal intelligence, teacher complaints of not listening, not completing work, disruptive behaviour.
pearls.hpc_character: Inattentive features: easily distracted, loses belongings, does not listen when spoken to directly, avoids tasks requiring sustained mental effort, poor organisation. Hyperactive-impulsive: runs/climbs excessively (or feels restless in adolescents), talks excessively, blurts out answers, cannot wait turn, interrupts others, fidgets/squirms constantly.
pearls.pmh_general: Comorbidities (common): oppositional defiant disorder (ODD — 50%), conduct disorder, anxiety, depression, learning disabilities (dyslexia, dyscalculia), ASD, tic disorders (Tourette's). Investigate: exclude vision and hearing problems. Exclude lead toxicity, thyroid disease, seizure disorder (absence epilepsy mimics inattention), iron deficiency anaemia.
pearls.exam_neuro: Rating scales are essential: Conners Rating Scale (parent + teacher versions). Vanderbilt Assessment Scale. SNAP-IV. These provide standardised, quantified assessment across settings. Child mental health assessment. IQ testing and academic assessment (to identify learning disabilities). Exclude neurological/medical causes.
pearls.meds_general: First-line in school-age children (≥6 years): methylphenidate (Ritalin) 5–20 mg 1–2× daily (short-acting) or extended-release. Response in 70% of children. Second-line: atomoxetine (non-stimulant, preferred if tics, anxiety, or substance misuse risk). Behavioural therapy is ALWAYS included — particularly important if <6 years (preferred over medication). School support: structured environment, preferential seating, extra time in exams. Parent training programmes. Medication monitoring: height, weight, pulse, BP (stimulants suppress appetite, raise HR/BP).

differentials.name: Anxiety Disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Inattention secondary to worry; present in specific contexts; somatic complaints; no hyperactivity

differentials.name: Absence Epilepsy
differentials.distinguishing: Brief staring episodes; EEG — 3 Hz spike and wave; no hyperactivity; provoked by hyperventilation

differentials.name: Hearing Impairment
differentials.distinguishing: Appears inattentive — not listening; audiometry; speech delay

differentials.name: Intellectual Disability
differentials.distinguishing: Global impairment; IQ <70; developmental delay across domains

differentials.name: Oppositional Defiant Disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Defiant behaviour toward authority; not difficulty sustaining attention; can overlap with ADHD

topic:meningococcal_disease.name: Meningococcal Disease
topic:meningococcal_disease.overview: Neisseria meningitidis causes two life-threatening syndromes: meningococcal meningitis and meningococcal septicaemia (often coexist). Serogroup A predominates in Nigeria's meningitis belt (northern states — epidemic during dry season Dec–June). Serogroup C causes outbreaks in southern Nigeria. Case fatality rate: 10–20%. Survivors: 20% have sequelae (deafness, limb loss, neurological).

pearls.hpc_onset: Fulminant meningococcaemia can kill in <24 hours from onset. The key warning sign: rapidly spreading non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash in a febrile child = EMERGENCY. Do NOT wait for LP or blood culture results — give IV benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone IMMEDIATELY.
pearls.sr_fever: Classic meningococcal presentation: prodrome (fever + myalgia + URTI-like illness 12–36h) → sudden deterioration → petechiae → purpura → shock (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome: bilateral adrenal haemorrhage + DIC + purpura fulminans).
pearls.exam_skin: Petechiae: non-blanching, 1–2 mm purple-red spots anywhere on body. Purpura: larger (>3 mm) — coalesce to form purpura fulminans (massive haemorrhagic necrosis of skin = DIC). Press glass over rash — if does NOT blanch = meningococcal until proven otherwise. Most important clinical skill in paediatric emergencies.
pearls.exam_general: Septic shock: cool, mottled extremities, capillary refill >2s, tachycardia, hypotension (late), confusion. Signs of DIC: bleeding from cannula sites, haematuria. Meningism (only 50–60% of cases — may be absent in overwhelming septicaemia).
pearls.ix_fbc: Blood culture (before antibiotics if POSSIBLE — but DO NOT DELAY antibiotics). PCR (meningococcal DNA in blood) — positive even after antibiotics. FBC: leucocytosis (or leucopaenia — worse prognosis), thrombocytopaenia (DIC). Coagulation: PT/APTT prolonged, fibrinogen low, D-dimers elevated = DIC. CRP, PCT markedly elevated. Meningococcal urinary antigen.
pearls.meds_general: IMMEDIATE IV ceftriaxone 80–100 mg/kg (or IV benzylpenicillin 300,000 units/kg/day if ceftriaxone unavailable). Resuscitation: 20 mL/kg 0.9% NaCl boluses — then reassess (careful with fluids in meningitis — SIADH risk; give freely in septic shock). Dexamethasone: give with first antibiotic dose (reduces meningitis sequelae — deafness). DIC: FFP + platelets if active bleeding. ICU: inotropes for refractory shock (noradrenaline). Notifiable disease — contact prophylaxis (rifampicin or ciprofloxacin) for household contacts.

differentials.name: ITP
differentials.distinguishing: Child WELL; flat purpura; isolated thrombocytopaenia; no fever/shock

differentials.name: HSP
differentials.distinguishing: Palpable purpura; lower limbs; arthritis; abdominal pain; normal platelets; normal CRP

differentials.name: Viral Haemorrhagic Fever
differentials.distinguishing: Epidemic context; travel; specific haemorrhagic features; specific serology

differentials.name: Bacterial Meningitis (other organisms)
differentials.distinguishing: Petechiae less common; pneumococcal/Hib identified on culture/antigen

topic:malaria_in_pregnancy_child.name: Malaria in Pregnancy — Neonatal & Congenital Malaria
topic:malaria_in_pregnancy_child.overview: Maternal malaria causes: low birth weight, preterm birth, stillbirth. Congenital malaria: placental transmission of parasites to fetus (rare). Neonatal malaria: presents at 5–30 days of life with fever, poor feeding, anaemia, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly — MUST consider in neonate born to malaria-endemic area. Distinguish from neonatal sepsis (may co-exist).

pearls.hpc_onset: Ask about: maternal history (malaria during pregnancy, treatment, IPTp uptake — sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine), delivery setting, birth weight, gestational age. Neonatal malaria: non-specific symptoms in first 2–4 weeks of life — fever or hypothermia, poor feeding, pallor, jaundice, irritability.
pearls.ix_fbc: Blood film + RDT in ALL neonates with unexplained fever, anaemia, or jaundice born to mothers in endemic areas. Malaria parasites in neonate = confirmed congenital/neonatal malaria. Simultaneously: blood culture (sepsis may co-exist). FBC (anaemia, thrombocytopaenia).
pearls.meds_general: Neonatal malaria treatment: IV artesunate (preferred if severe) or oral ACT (artemether-lumefantrine) if well. Do NOT use primaquine in neonates (G6PD deficiency risk, haemolysis). Maternal prophylaxis: IPTp with SP at 2nd and 3rd trimester (reduces malaria burden and LBW). LLIN (long-lasting insecticidal nets) — all pregnant women and children under 5.

symptoms_signs: Fever or hypothermia (neonates may not mount fever)
clinical_features.key_point: Neonatal malaria is rare but must be considered in endemic areas. Blood film is the investigation — do not miss it.

topic:neonatal_hypoglycaemia.name: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia
topic:neonatal_hypoglycaemia.overview: Blood glucose <2.6 mmol/L in a neonate. Most common metabolic emergency in neonatal period. High-risk groups: LGA (IDM — infant of diabetic mother), SGA (IUGR), premature infants, infants with perinatal stress. Prolonged or recurrent hypoglycaemia causes brain damage.

pearls.hpc_onset: At-risk neonates: IDM (mother has gestational or pre-existing diabetes — fetal hyperinsulinism from maternal hyperglycaemia). SGA/IUGR (reduced glycogen stores). Premature infants (immature gluconeogenesis). Perinatal asphyxia. Erythroblastosis fetalis. LGA: macrosomic baby with obese/diabetic mother.
pearls.hpc_character: Symptoms: jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, temperature instability, apnoea, seizures, coma. Asymptomatic hypoglycaemia is common in at-risk groups — routine screening mandatory. Persistent hypoglycaemia (requiring glucose infusion rate >10–12 mg/kg/min): suspect hyperinsulinism (IDM, Beckwith-Wiedemann, KATP channelopathy).
pearls.ix_fbc: Bedside: glucometer (confirm with lab glucose — glucometers inaccurate at very low levels). Lab glucose: <2.6 mmol/L = treat. Critical samples (if persistent/severe): insulin, cortisol, GH, lactate, ammonia, free fatty acids, ketones, acylcarnitine profile — all taken DURING hypoglycaemia before treatment for maximum diagnostic yield.
