pearls.meds_general: Asymptomatic, able to feed: early breastfeeding/formula, recheck glucose in 30–60 min. Symptomatic or glucose <1.5 mmol/L: IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg bolus, then 6–8 mg/kg/min continuous infusion. Increase GIR by 2 mg/kg/min every 30 min until glucose stable. Persistent hyperinsulinism: diazoxide (opens KATP channels), octreotide, glucagon. Surgical: near-total pancreatectomy (focal KATP hyperinsulinism).

topic:nephritic_syndrome_child.name: Nephritic Syndrome — Childhood
topic:nephritic_syndrome_child.overview: Clinical syndrome of haematuria + hypertension + oliguria + oedema (mild) with variable proteinuria. Key cause in children: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Other causes: IgA nephropathy, membranoproliferative GN, lupus nephritis, Henoch-Schönlein nephritis. Distinguished from nephrotic syndrome by the presence of haematuria and hypertension.

pearls.hpc_onset: PSGN: 1–3 weeks after streptococcal throat infection, OR 3–6 weeks after streptococcal skin infection (impetigo — common in Nigeria). Child presents with: cola/tea-coloured urine (haematuria), facial puffiness (oedema), reduced urine output, hypertension. Age: 5–12 years.
pearls.hpc_character: Haematuria: tea/cola coloured (glomerular haematuria — RBC casts). Hypertension: may cause headache, visual disturbance, or encephalopathy (hypertensive emergency). Oliguria: hallmark of acute nephritis. Oedema: periorbital first, then mild generalised (less massive than nephrotic). Proteinuria: usually mild-moderate (sub-nephrotic).
pearls.sr_urinary: Urine dipstick: blood +++ (haematuria), protein + or ++ (proteinuria, not nephrotic range). Urine microscopy: dysmorphic RBCs (hallmark of glomerular haematuria), RBC casts (pathognomonic of nephritis), granular casts.
pearls.ix_fbc: ASO titre (elevated in 80% of throat infections, less sensitive for skin — use anti-DNase B for impetigo). C3 complement: markedly LOW in PSGN (consumption by immune complex) — KEY FINDING. C4: normal in PSGN (distinguishes from SLE where C4 also low). Throat swab / skin swab culture. Renal biopsy: rarely needed in typical PSGN (clinical diagnosis). Biopsy if: atypical age, prolonged complement depression (>8 weeks — suspect MPGN or lupus), rapid progression, nephrotic range proteinuria.
pearls.meds_general: PSGN: self-limiting in most cases. Supportive: fluid restriction (oliguria), low-sodium diet, antihypertensives (amlodipine, nifedipine). Diuretics (frusemide) for oedema/hypertension. Penicillin (eradicate GAS — secondary prevention, does not change course of nephritis). Hypertensive encephalopathy: urgent IV antihypertensives (hydralazine, labetalol). Prognosis: excellent in PSGN — complement normalises in 8 weeks, haematuria resolves in 6–12 months.

differentials.name: Nephrotic Syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Massive proteinuria (3+/4+); low albumin; no haematuria; normal blood pressure; normal C3

differentials.name: IgA Nephropathy
differentials.distinguishing: Haematuria DURING or immediately after URTI (synpharyngitic — not delayed); normal C3; recurrent

differentials.name: Lupus Nephritis
differentials.distinguishing: Adolescent female; ANA/dsDNA positive; low C3 AND C4; multisystem involvement

differentials.name: HSP Nephritis
differentials.distinguishing: Palpable purpura; arthritis; abdominal pain; IgA mesangial deposits; normal C3

differentials.name: Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome (HUS)
differentials.distinguishing: Triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopaenia + AKI; bloody diarrhoea (E. coli O157:H7); Coombs negative

topic:rickettsial_disease.name: Rickettsial Diseases — African Tick Bite Fever
topic:rickettsial_disease.overview: Obligate intracellular gram-negative bacteria transmitted by arthropod vectors. African tick bite fever (Rickettsia africae): most common rickettsial disease in sub-Saharan Africa including Nigeria. Epidemic typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii): louse-borne, occurs in conflict/displaced populations (northern Nigeria). Scrub typhus less common in West Africa.

pearls.hpc_onset: Ask about: tick exposure (bush walking, rural farm areas), louse infestation (overcrowded living, displaced communities), rash characteristics, eschar (painless black necrotic skin lesion at site of tick bite — pathognomonic of tick bite fever).
pearls.sr_fever: African tick bite fever: fever + eschar + regional lymphadenopathy + maculopapular rash. Epidemic typhus: high fever, severe headache, diffuse maculopapular rash (starts on trunk → spreads centrifugally), confusion, myalgia — no eschar. Weil-Felix test (positive in most rickettsial diseases but non-specific). Specific: Rickettsia serology (IFA).
pearls.meds_general: Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for ALL rickettsial diseases. Children <8 years: azithromycin (avoids tetracycline dental staining). Chloramphenicol: alternative if doxycycline unavailable. Treatment duration: 7–10 days (until afebrile ≥3 days). Do NOT delay treatment — clinical diagnosis should prompt empirical therapy.

topic:enuresis.name: Nocturnal Enuresis (Bedwetting)
topic:enuresis.overview: Involuntary urination during sleep in a child ≥5 years of age. Primary enuresis: never been dry. Secondary enuresis: relapse after ≥6 months of dryness. Prevalence: 15–20% at age 5, decreasing spontaneously (15% per year). Most is primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis (MNE) — highly responsive to treatment. Important: exclude secondary causes in all cases.

pearls.hpc_onset: Primary MNE: most common, no daytime symptoms, normal bladder function. Secondary enuresis: NEW onset after dry period = always investigate. Common causes of secondary enuresis: UTI, diabetes mellitus (polyuria), diabetes insipidus, constipation (loaded rectum compresses bladder), psychosocial stress, sexual abuse.
pearls.hpc_character: Daytime symptoms (urgency, frequency, incontinence) in addition to enuresis: suggests overactive bladder, UTI, or structural abnormality. Frequency of wet nights. Urine output pattern. Fluid intake (especially evening). Caffeine intake (tea, fizzy drinks — diuretic). Stool history (constipation very common association).
pearls.ix_fbc: Urine dipstick + MC&S (UTI). Blood glucose (DM). Renal USS (structural anomaly — only if daytime symptoms or UTI). No need for routine urodynamics in uncomplicated primary MNE.
pearls.meds_general: Simple lifestyle measures first: limit evening fluids (last drink 1 hour before bed), void before bed, avoid caffeine. Enuresis alarm (bedwetting alarm): most effective long-term treatment — 70–80% success, low relapse. Desmopressin (DDAVP): synthetic ADH — reduces urine production overnight. Tablet/melt 0.2–0.4 mg before bed. Use when rapid effect needed or alarm not practical. Combine alarm + desmopressin for best results. Treat constipation (if present). Imipramine: third-line (side effect profile).

topic:downs_syndrome.name: Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21)
topic:downs_syndrome.overview: Most common chromosomal abnormality in live births. Incidence: 1 in 700–1000 live births, higher with advanced maternal age. Trisomy 21 (non-disjunction): 94%. Translocation: 4%. Mosaic: 2%. Recognisable at birth by characteristic features. Multiple system involvement — children require comprehensive multidisciplinary care.

pearls.hpc_onset: Prenatal: maternal serum screening (PAPP-A + beta-hCG + NT ultrasound — first trimester), followed by NIPT (non-invasive prenatal testing) or diagnostic amniocentesis/CVS. Postnatal diagnosis: clinical features at birth + confirmatory karyotype.
pearls.exam_general: Characteristic features: flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, Brushfield spots (iris), macroglossia, single palmar crease (Simian crease), wide sandal gap (1st–2nd toe), hypotonia (cardinal feature at birth), small ears, short stature. NOT all features present in every child.
pearls.pmh_general: Mandatory screening at diagnosis and follow-up: CHD (40–50% — most common: AV canal/AVSD, VSD, ASD, TOF — ECHO at diagnosis), hearing loss (conductive + sensorineural — audiometry), vision (squint, cataracts, refractive — ophthalmology), hypothyroidism (TFTs annually), atlanto-axial instability (cervical spine X-ray before contact sports/anaesthesia), leukaemia risk (transient myeloproliferative disorder, ALL — 20× increased risk), coeliac disease screening, Alzheimer's disease (adults).
pearls.meds_general: No curative treatment. Comprehensive multidisciplinary care: physiotherapy (hypotonia, motor delay), speech therapy (language delay, feeding difficulties), occupational therapy, early intervention programmes, inclusive schooling. Cardiac surgery (CHD). Hearing aids. Thyroid replacement (hypothyroidism). Counselling parents: life expectancy now >60 years with good care; quality of life significantly improved with early intervention.

differentials.name: Other Chromosomal Trisomies
differentials.distinguishing: Trisomy 18 (Edwards) — severe malformations, rocker-bottom feet; Trisomy 13 (Patau) — midline defects, polydactyly; karyotype confirms

differentials.name: Zellweger Syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Peroxisomal disorder; hypotonia + facial features; very poor prognosis; VLCFA elevated

differentials.name: Neonatal Hypothyroidism
differentials.distinguishing: Hypotonia + macroglossia; TFTs abnormal; no chromosomal features; Down's can have both

topic:haemolytic_disease_newborn.name: Haemolytic Disease of the Newborn (HDN)
topic:haemolytic_disease_newborn.overview: Maternal alloantibodies cross the placenta and haemolyse fetal/neonatal red cells. Causes: Rh incompatibility (Rh-negative mother, Rh-positive baby — anti-D antibodies), ABO incompatibility (mother type O, baby type A or B — anti-A/B IgG). Rh disease: more severe (subsequent pregnancies worse). ABO disease: can occur in first pregnancy, usually milder.

pearls.hpc_onset: Jaundice within 24 hours of birth = pathological until proven otherwise. Key question: blood group of mother (Rh-negative? Type O?) and father. History of previous affected pregnancies, intrauterine transfusions, previous anti-D prophylaxis.
pearls.ix_fbc: Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT/Coombs test): POSITIVE — indicates antibody-coated RBCs (haemolytic disease). Blood group of mother and baby. Maternal antibody screen (indirect Coombs). SBR (serum bilirubin): plot on Bhutani nomogram — hour-specific phototherapy threshold. Hb (anaemia from haemolysis). Reticulocyte count (elevated — compensatory).
pearls.meds_general: Phototherapy: immediate. Exchange transfusion: if SBR rising despite phototherapy or signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy. Rh prophylaxis (PREVENTION): anti-D immunoglobulin to Rh-negative mothers — at 28 weeks, at 34 weeks, and within 72 hours of delivery of Rh-positive baby. Also after any sensitising event (miscarriage, amniocentesis). IV immunoglobulin (IVIG): may reduce need for exchange transfusion in ABO disease.

topic:schistosomiasis_child.name: Schistosomiasis — Childhood
topic:schistosomiasis_child.overview: Parasitic infection caused by Schistosoma species. S. haematobium (urogenital): most common in Nigeria — transmitted via freshwater contact with infected snails. S. mansoni (intestinal/hepatic). Endemic in Niger Delta, riverside communities, irrigation areas. Children are heavily exposed through swimming/bathing in freshwater.

pearls.hpc_onset: Katayama fever (acute schistosomiasis): 4–8 weeks after initial heavy exposure — fever, urticaria, cough, hepatosplenomegaly, eosinophilia. Chronic urogenital schistosomiasis: painless terminal haematuria ('blood in urine after passing last drop') — often normalised by affected communities ('a sign of growing up' in boys).
pearls.sr_urinary: Terminal haematuria (S. haematobium): blood at END of urination — characteristic. Distinguishes from upper urinary tract bleeding (blood throughout stream) and bladder cancer (gross haematuria, older patients). Dysuria, frequency. Hydronephrosis (ureteric obstruction — chronic). Bladder wall thickening and calcification (chronic — 'sandy patches' on cystoscopy/USS).
pearls.ix_fbc: Eosinophilia (peripheral blood) — prominent in acute and chronic infection. Urine filtration (terminal urine sample — collect last 10 mL of midday urine): Schistosoma haematobium eggs with terminal spine. Stool Kato-Katz (S. mansoni eggs with lateral spine). Serology (ELISA): sensitive in early/light infection. Urine dipstick: haematuria + proteinuria. USS abdomen/pelvis: bladder wall thickening, hydronephrosis, hepatosplenomegaly (portal hypertension — S. mansoni).
pearls.meds_general: Praziquantel: 40 mg/kg single dose (or 2 × 20 mg/kg on same day). Safe, highly effective, well tolerated. Treat all infected children. Mass drug administration (MDA) in schools in endemic areas (WHO strategy). Prevention: avoid freshwater exposure, water treatment, snail control, health education. Follow-up urine microscopy at 6 weeks post-treatment to confirm cure.

drug:artemether_lumefantrine.name: Artemether-Lumefantrine (Coartem / Lonart)
drug:artemether_lumefantrine.dose: Weight-based, twice daily × 3 days: 5–14 kg: 1 tablet (20mg/120mg). 15–24 kg: 2 tablets. 25–34 kg: 3 tablets. ≥35 kg: 4 tablets. Give with fatty food (enhances lumefantrine absorption — peanuts, milk).
drug:artemether_lumefantrine.nigerian_pearl: Most widely used ACT in Nigeria. Available at all tiers of health care. Ensure full 6-dose course — incomplete courses increase resistance risk. Advise caregivers on importance of completing even when fever resolves.

drug:oral_rehydration_salts.name: Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) — WHO Low-Osmolality
drug:oral_rehydration_salts.composition: Sodium 75 mmol/L, Chloride 65 mmol/L, Glucose 75 mmol/L, Potassium 20 mmol/L, Citrate 10 mmol/L. Osmolality 245 mOsm/L.
drug:oral_rehydration_salts.dose: Plan A (no dehydration): 5–10 mL/kg after each loose stool. Plan B (some dehydration): 75 mL/kg over 4 hours.
drug:oral_rehydration_salts.resomal: ReSoMal (for SAM): lower sodium (45 mmol/L), higher potassium (40 mmol/L), magnesium added — prevents fatal electrolyte shifts when standard ORS given to malnourished children. NEVER use standard ORS in SAM.
drug:oral_rehydration_salts.nigerian_pearl: ORS sachets available at all PHC levels. Demonstrate preparation to caregivers (1 sachet in 1 litre clean water). Teaspoon feeding for vomiting children (5–10 mL every 2–3 minutes). Continue breastfeeding. Zinc supplementation alongside ORS.

drug:ceftriaxone_paediatric.name: Ceftriaxone (Rocephin) — Paediatric Dosing
drug:ceftriaxone_paediatric.dose: Meningitis: 100 mg/kg/day IV divided 12-hourly. Sepsis/pneumonia: 50–80 mg/kg/day once daily IV/IM. Neonatal sepsis: 50 mg/kg/day (CAUTION: displaces bilirubin — AVOID in jaundiced neonates or with IV calcium-containing fluids — precipitates in lungs/kidneys).
contraindications: Do NOT give with IV calcium (precipitation — fatal in neonates)
drug:ceftriaxone_paediatric.nigerian_pearl: Widely available at secondary/tertiary level. Excellent CSF penetration — drug of choice for bacterial meningitis. In neonates with suspected meningitis + jaundice: use cefotaxime instead of ceftriaxone.

drug:prednisolone_paediatric.name: Prednisolone — Paediatric Uses
drug:prednisolone_paediatric.dose_nephrotic: 2 mg/kg/day (max 60 mg) × 4–6 weeks, then alternate day × 4–6 weeks (ISKDC standard protocol)
drug:prednisolone_paediatric.side_effects: Cushing's features (weight gain, moon face, striae), growth suppression, hypertension, hyperglycaemia, immunosuppression (increased infection risk — especially varicella), osteoporosis, mood changes.
drug:prednisolone_paediatric.nigerian_pearl: Monitor blood pressure and urinalysis at each visit in children on prolonged steroids. Varicella vaccine before starting immunosuppression if available. Calcium + Vitamin D supplementation for children on long-term steroids.

pearl:exam_cardiovascular.content: Paediatric cardiovascular exam: Position (left lateral for apex, sitting forward for aortic regurgitation murmur). Inspection: precordial bulge (chronic cardiomegaly), surgical scars. Palpation: apex beat (normal position = 4th ICS midclavicular line <7 years; 5th ICS <12 years), thrills, heaves. Auscultation: S1 and S2 (fixed split S2 = ASD; loud S2 = pulmonary hypertension). Murmur: grade 1–6, character, location, radiation. Peripheral: pulses (radio-femoral delay = coarctation), capillary refill, oedema.

pearl:exam_chest.content: Paediatric chest exam: Count RR for ONE FULL MINUTE (child calm — most sensitive single vital sign). WHO thresholds: <2mo ≥60, 2–11mo ≥50, 1–5yr ≥40, >5yr ≥30. Inspect: recession (subcostal > intercostal > suprasternal — severity escalates), nasal flaring, grunting, head bobbing. Palpate: tactile fremitus. Percuss: resonance vs dullness. Auscultate: equal air entry, adventitious sounds (wheeze = lower airway, stridor = upper airway, crackles = alveolar/small airway).

pearl:pmh_general.content: Paediatric past medical history must cover: (1) Antenatal history (infections, medications, alcohol, hypertension, diabetes in mother). (2) Birth history (gestation, mode of delivery, Apgar scores, NICU admission, birth weight). (3) Neonatal problems (jaundice, sepsis, seizures, HIE). (4) Previous admissions. (5) Chronic illnesses. (6) Surgeries. (7) Allergies (drug + food + environmental). (8) Immunisation history. All paediatric histories require this foundation — it often unlocks the diagnosis.

pearl:shx_social.content: Paediatric social history: (1) Household composition — who lives at home, primary carer, siblings. (2) Housing (overcrowding, ventilation — TB/meningitis risk). (3) Income and employment (poverty → malnutrition, delayed presentation). (4) Water source (tap vs well vs river — typhoid, cholera, schistosomiasis). (5) Mosquito net usage (malaria). (6) Schooling (attendance, performance). (7) Diet — 24-hour recall, food security, feeding practices (breastfeeding, complementary). (8) Tobacco/alcohol in home (passive exposure).

pearl:fhx.content: Family history in paediatrics: (1) Consanguinity (increases risk of autosomal recessive conditions — metabolic diseases, haemoglobinopathies, immune deficiency). (2) Siblings with similar illness (genetic, infectious). (3) SCD/thalassaemia in family (genotype parents). (4) TB contact in household (smear-positive adult = main transmission route). (5) Epilepsy/febrile seizures (genetic susceptibility). (6) Congenital heart disease. (7) Cancer. (8) Atopy (asthma, eczema, hay fever — family history doubles child's risk of asthma).

pearl:ix_cxr.content: CXR systematic reading in children: (1) Projection + rotation. (2) Airways: tracheal deviation, subglottic narrowing (steeple sign = croup), mediastinal widening. (3) Bones: rib fractures (NAI), vertebral anomalies. (4) Cardiac: cardiothoracic ratio (>0.55 = cardiomegaly). Boot-shaped = TOF. Egg-on-side = TGA. (5) Lungs: lobar consolidation (bacterial pneumonia), bilateral perihilar (viral/PCP), miliary nodules (TB), hyperinflation (asthma/bronchiolitis), pleural effusion. (6) Diaphragm: free air under diaphragm = perforation.

pearl:meds_general.content: Drug prescribing in paediatrics: (1) Always WEIGHT-BASED dosing (mg/kg) — never adult doses without adjustment. (2) Check maximum dose — weight-based dose can exceed adult maximum (e.g. amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day max = 3g/day). (3) Age restrictions: doxycycline (avoid <8 years — teeth staining), quinolones (caution <18 years — tendon toxicity), aspirin (avoid <16 years — Reye's syndrome), metformin (avoid <10 years). (4) Formulation: liquid for infants/young children; tablets can be crushed if no modified-release. (5) Document: dose (mg), frequency, route, duration, max dose.

guideline:epi_nigeria.title: Nigerian Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI) — Current Schedule

schedule.9_months: MCV1 (Measles vaccine), Yellow Fever (single dose, lifelong), Vitamin A (first dose)

guideline:epi_nigeria.pearl: Vaccination card must be checked at every paediatric consultation. Missed vaccines should be given at the earliest opportunity (catch-up). BCG scar check at 6 weeks — repeat if no scar. Seasonal: Meningococcal A vaccine during epidemic season campaigns in northern Nigeria. HPV vaccine (girls 9–14) — being rolled out in phases.
guideline:epi_nigeria.cold_chain: Vaccines must be stored at 2–8°C. VVM (Vaccine Vial Monitor) on each vial — do NOT use if VVM past endpoint. Open vial policy: multi-dose vials must be used within 4h (or discarded at end of session).

guideline:pedialyte_rehydration.title: WHO Oral Rehydration Therapy — Plan A/B/C Summary
guideline:pedialyte_rehydration.plan_a: No dehydration: continue feeding, increase fluids at home. ORS 5–10 mL/kg per loose stool. Zinc 10–20 mg/day × 10–14 days. Return if worse.
guideline:pedialyte_rehydration.plan_b: Some dehydration: ORS 75 mL/kg over 4 hours in facility. Observe. After rehydration, reassess and move to Plan A. If cannot take ORS (vomiting): nasogastric ORS 20 mL/kg/hour.
guideline:pedialyte_rehydration.plan_c: Severe dehydration: IV access → Ringer's Lactate (preferred) or 0.9% NaCl 100 mL/kg. <12 months: 30 mL/kg over 1h + 70 mL/kg over 5h. ≥12 months: 30 mL/kg over 30min + 70 mL/kg over 2.5h. Reassess every 30 min — if improving continue; if not improving consider septic shock.
guideline:pedialyte_rehydration.key_principle: ReSoMal must be used for SAM children — NOT standard ORS. Breastfeeding continues throughout.

guideline:bts_asthma_acute.title: BTS/SIGN Acute Asthma in Children — Treatment Stepwise
guideline:bts_asthma_acute.mild: PEFR >75% predicted. SABA (salbutamol) 2–4 puffs via spacer every 4h. Oral prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg if not improving.
guideline:bts_asthma_acute.moderate: PEFR 50–75%. Salbutamol 10 puffs spacer or 2.5–5 mg nebulised every 20–30 min × 3. Prednisolone oral. SpO₂ target >94%.
guideline:bts_asthma_acute.severe: PEFR 33–50%. Continuous salbutamol nebulisation + ipratropium bromide. IV magnesium sulphate 25–40 mg/kg over 20 min (max 2g). IV salbutamol if nebulisation failing. High-flow oxygen.
guideline:bts_asthma_acute.life_threatening: PEFR <33%, silent chest. Senior/ICU input immediately. IV magnesium. IV salbutamol infusion. Consider NIPPV. Intubation (last resort — very difficult in acute asthma, high risk).
guideline:bts_asthma_acute.nigerian_note: Oxygen concentrators widely used in Nigeria — ensure adequate flow (6–8 L/min for driving nebuliser). Salbutamol via spacer equivalent to nebulised salbutamol and preferred when nebuliser unavailable. Aminophylline IV: third-line option (still used in Nigeria — narrow therapeutic window, monitor levels and ECG).
